lawyer: Kamal-ul-Alam, Senior Advocate with Sikder Mahmudur Razi, Advocate ------ For the Plaintiff. Moudud Ahmed with Mizanul Haque Chowdhury with Hasan Mohammad Reyad with Razaul Karim, Advocates ------ For the Applicant.
parties:
Bank Asia Limited ------ Plaintiff-Applicant
Vs.
MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' and others ------ Defendants
full_judgment:
AFM Abdur Rahman, J: This suit has appeared in the list as item No. 4 under the head of order.

2. In the instant suit, filed by the plaintiff Bank Asia Limited against the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' Ex. 'Vanashin Atlantic' and one M/s Al-Madina Enterprise, a proprietor-ship concern of Md Giasuddin and others, two applications have been filed for addition of parties, one being filed by M/s Khawaja Garibullah Shah Trading and the other application has been filed by Haji Mohammad Nurul Amin and one Mohammad Ali jointly.

3. The factual aspects and the law involved in these applications being the same and identical, this court has taken these applications for disposal analogously and now disposed of by this single order.

4. In the first application, dated 17-7-2016, filed by M/s Khawaja Garibullah Shah Trading, it has been stated that the applicant is a trader which deals in buying and selling steel plates of various scrap vessels. One Mr. Giasuddin is the proprietor of the defendant No. 2 who has some other enterprises under the name and style M/s Shah Amanat Iron Mart and M/s Tanha Steel. The said Mr. Giasuddin from time to time received money in the name of his enterprises from the applicant for the purpose of selling steel plates to the applicant and accordingly received Taka 4,60,00,000 up to 9-12-2013 in cash as well as by cheques from the applicant, for supplying steel plate of scrap vessels. But those enterprises failed to deliver any steel plates and lastly the said Mr Giasuddin assured the applicant that his enterprise namely M/s Al-Madina Enterprise since importing scrap vessel 'MT Atlanta', he will deliver steel plates against all the money he received from the applicant. Pursuant to the request of Mr Giasuddin, the applicant further paid an amount of 9,90,00,000 for the said purpose of purchasing steel plates of the said vessel 'MT Atlanta'. The said amount was paid through cheques in favour of M/s Al-Madina Enterprise and Shah Amanat Iron Mart, as requested by Mr Giasuddin who gave written undertaking on 20-12-2013 to deliver six thousand metric tons of steel plates from the said scrap vessel 'MT Atlanta' within six months.

5. It has been further stated in the instant application that for the reason of the facts stated as above, the applicant has obtained an interest in the said scrap vessel namely 'MT Atlanta' and hence, the applicant is entitled to be added as defendant No. 3A in the instant Admiralty Suit, otherwise the applicant shall be non-suited without any remedy and shall suffer irreparable loss and injury.

6. This applicant M/s Khawaja Garibullah Shah Trading has submitted different documents by way of list of documents and also through the supplementary list of documents.

7. The second application has been filed by Haji Mohammad Nurul Amin and Mohammad Ali jointly, wherein it has been stated that the applicants are required to be added as defendant 3A-3L in the instant suit as the applicants are interested party in the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' since the applicants along with ten others have filed Admiralty Suit No. 35 of 2016 against the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' and 17 others with a prayer for a declaratory decree for proportionate ownership of the plaintiffs in the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' (IMO No. 9014834, Flag; Union of Comoros), now lying at Sitakunda Fouzdarhat Shipyard, Lalbegh South Sitalpur, Sonaichari, Sitakunda, Chittagong, or in the alternative a decree for realizing a sum of Taka 34,65,71,341 only from the defendants to be passed in favour of the plaintiff against the principal defendants jointly and severally and further a decree may be passed granting pendentilite interest on the decretal amount at the rate of 20% per annum from the date of filing of the suit till the date of actual realization of the decretal amount along with the cost of the suit and any other relief which may be granted to the plaintiff as found to be entitled to in law and equity. It has been further stated that the said suit was admitted by this court on 10-5-2016 wherein the plaintiff of the instant suit, Bank Asia Limited, has been made as defendant No. 7.

8. It has been further stated in the instant 2nd application that the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' was imported by M/s Al-Madia Enterprise to sell the scrap iron of the vessel to the iron and steel merchants. The applicant No. 1 of this 2n application is the proprietor of Al-Rafi Trade International and Shakil Trading and Company and being scrap iron trader, he has paid an amount of Taka 7,00,00,000 to Mr Giasuddin Kusum, proprietor of Al-Madina Enterprise through different cheques, to purchase the scrap iron obtainable from the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic'.

9. It has been further stated that the applicant No. 2 of the 2nd application Mohammad Ali is also a scrap iron trader who has paid Taka 2,75,00,000 to Mr Giasuddin Kusum in order to purchase scrap iron from the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' through different cheques and since the Bank Asia Limited filed the instant suit and trying to obtain a decree as against the interest of the applicants, the applicants are required to be added in the instant suit as defendants in order to defend their interest, being necessary and proper parties, since without the presence of the applicants any prospective decree in favour of the plaintiff might affect the rights and interests of the applicants adversely, else the applicants will suffer irreparable loss and injury.

10. Several documents have been filed along with the 2nd application by way of list of documents and supplementary list of documents.

11. Against both the applications the Bank Asia Limited filed separate written objection against the prayer for addition of parties, wherein the written objection filed against the first application states that the instant two applications are frivolous applications, filed with an ulterior motive for wrongful gain at the behest of some vested person, who are trying to grab the defendant No. 1 vessel at any cost by adopting all fraudulent means. The applicants have no cause of action against the vessel 'MT Atlanta' and, as such, they are not necessary parties for the adjudication of the instant cause of action of the plaintiff raised in the instant suit. The claim of payment of money to Mr. Md Gias Uddin through bank cheque, have been proved to be false. The undertaking dated 20-12-2013 alleged to have been issued and signed by Mr Md Giasuddin as proprietor of Al-Madina Enterprise and the letter head of the Al-Madina Enterprise is forged and manufactured one which would be evident from a comparison with the admitted signature of the said Mr Md Giasuddin appearing in the account opening form of the Account No. 0383-300-0050 in the name of his proprietorship firm M/s Al-Madina Enterprise, maintained with the plaintiff Bank Asia and his application dated 11-11-2013 before the plaintiff Bank Asia Limited for opening LC for importing the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic'.

12. It has been further stated that the applicants of the 1st application stated that on the request of Mr. Md Giasuddin the applicants paid him a further amount of Taka 9,90,00,000 through various cheques including cheque No. 5917701 dated 17-11-2013 for an amount of Taka 5,00,00,000 and cheque No. 5917702 dated 15-11-2013 for an amount of Taka 3,00,00,000 drawn on Prime Bank Limited, Halishahor Branch, Chittagong and the photocopy of those cheques have been submitted by way of list of documents before this court. Pursuant to that claim the plaintiff Bank Asia Limited made a quarry before the said Prime Bank Limited through their letter dated 27-7-2016 which informed the plaintiff Bank Asia Limited that the said cheques have never been placed for encashment with their bank which established the facts that the applicant of the 1st application has made the aforesaid false statement on solemn oath in its affidavit. Moreover, the signature appearing on those two cheques differ from each other which proves that the said cheques are forged and subsequently created with a view to make wrongful gain and, as such, the 1st application for addition of party is liable to be rejected.

13. It has been further stated in the written objection against the 1st application that even the claim of the applicant if for argument sake is taken as lawful even then the claim is not against the vessel as a whole, but only the claim for purchase of scrap steel plates which does not make the applicants as entitled in law to claim any interest in the defendant No. 1 vessel and, as such, the applicant is not a necessary party in the instant suit for which the application is liable to be rejected.

14. In the second objection filed by the plaintiff against the 2n application the materials claims of the application have been denied and further inter-alia stated that the statement as has been made in the application are all highly malafide, purposeful and ill motivated since none of the alleged payment has actually been made to the said Mr Giasuddin.

15. It has been further stated that the applicants are neither necessary nor proper parties nor they are persons interested in the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' since the present Admiralty Suit has been filed for recovery of damages, compensation, possession on the basis of contract between the plaintiff and the L/C issuing bank and the defendant No. 2 as the L/C opener for the purchase of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' under the letter of credit dated 19-11-2013 to which the present applicants have not privity of contract. The applicants are so called intending purchaser of scrap iron to be obtained from the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' as has been claimed, but the said vessel being presently a floating vessel and not a scrap one and, as such, no interest has been accrued to the applicant in the said vessel. Therefore, the applicants are neither necessary nor a proper party nor its presence in the suit is necessary for proper adjudication of the dispute between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 2 M/s Al-Madina Enterprise, being a proprietary concern of Mr. Md. Gias Uddin.

16. It has been further stated that the applicants although have claimed they have paid money to M/s AI-Madina Enterprise and Shah Amanat Iron Mart, proprietor being Giasuddin Kusum, to purchase scrap iron from the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic', but the applicants have failed to produce any agreement to support their assertions that they have paid money to purchase scrap iron obtainable from the vessel 'MT Atlanta' ex 'Vinashin Atlantic' upon its scrapping. Therefore, the assertions are baseless, ill motivated and purposeful and they are trying to be added as party in the instant suit for illegal gain and, as such, the instant application for addition of party is liable to be rejected.

17. It has been further stated that the applicants have filed Admiralty Suit No. 35 of 2016, making the plaintiff of this suit as defendant No. 7, along with eight other plaintiffs but those eight other persons have not filed any application for addition of party in the instant suit. Therefore the purpose of those two applications are not bonafide and as such, the instant application is required to be rejected with cost.

18. The learned Advocate Mr Moudud Ahmed appeared as a senior counsel to support the two applications and submitted that the applicants have paid huge amount of money to the defendant No. 2 of the instant suit by way of cash and bank transaction, the copy of those cheques are filed along with the application by way of list of documents, wherefrom it appears that the defendant No. 2 have received those huge amount of money as consideration of the scrap iron to be obtained from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' . In support of such sell the said Mr Giasuddin executed two separate contracts one in favour of the first applicant and other in favour of the second applicants, wherein the fact of sale and purchase of scrap iron from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' has been established. In the instant suit the plaintiff Bank Asia has claimed a decree of damage and compensation against the principal defendants on the ground that L/C has been opened through them by the said Mr Giasuddin, the proprietor of the defendant No. 2 for the purpose of purchase and import of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta'. Therefore the claim of the plaintiff in the instant suit and against the defendant No. 1 vessel and the claim of the applicants against the defendant No. 1 vessel are similar and identical and if the applicants are not present in the instant suit and the suit is decreed only in favour of the plaintiff Bank Asia, then the vital issue of proportionate ownership of the applicants in the vessel 'MT Atlanta' will not be adjudicated causing serious complication with the issue of ownership of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' which has been claimed in Admiralty Suit No. 35 of 2016, being pending in this court. Therefore, the presence of the applicants in the instant suit is very much required for the purpose of adjudicating the real question involved in the suit.

19. The learned senior counsel Mr. Moudud Ahmed, further submitted that the documents, as have been filed by the applicants along with the application, clearly proved the fact that the payment has been made by the applicants to the defendant No. 2 proprietor being Mr Giasuddin for the only purpose of purchasing scrap iron, to be obtained from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' and therefore by paying money the applicants and all eight others have obtained an interest in the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' for which they are entitled to proceed against the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' itself for which the applicants along with eight others have initiated the Admiralty Suit No. 35 of 2016 in this Admiralty court which has been admitted by this court for which the interest of the applicants in the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' has already been established. Therefore, the applicants are necessary parties to be added in the instant suit.

20. The learned senior counsel Mr. Moudud Ahmed finally submitted that huge amount of money since have been paid by the applicants to the said Mr. Giasuddin proprietor of the defendant No. 2, for the purchase of the scrap iron to be obtained from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' imported by him for the purpose of scrapping the same and, as such, if the applicants are not made party in the instant suit they will face irreparable loss and injury and will be deprived off from their legitimate claim. Therefore, the applicants are required to be made parties in the instant suit.

21. On the other hand the learned Advocate Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam appeared as senior counsel on behalf of the plaintiff Bank Asia, who while taken this court through different decisions of our apex court and also from other jurisdiction, strenuously argued that the presence of the instant applicants are not required for the purpose of adjudication of the real question involved in the cause of action in the instant suit, since the plaintiff in the instant suit has claimed that it has opened a L/C on the request of the defendant No. 2 Mr. Giasuddin for the purpose of purchase and import of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' and since the said defendant No. 2 Mr. Giasuddin failed to repay the L/C amount the plaintiff is entitled to realize the damage and compensation not only from the defendant No. 2 in a proceeding impersonal but also against the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' in a proceeding in rem and, as such, the plaintiff has initiated the instant suit in this Admiralty Court against the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' and also the defendant No. 2 Mr Giasuddin, which is both in action in rem and in personam. The question to be decided in the instant suit involves the issue of opening of L/C by the defendant No. 2 Mr Giasuddin through the plaintiff Bank Asia to purchase the defendant No. 1 vessel and upon such adjudication the issue of realization of damage and compensation will be resolved. This question is entirely remained in between the plaintiff and the said defendant No. 2 Mr Giasuddin upon a contract executed in between the plaintiff Bank and the defendant No. 2 to which the applicants have no privity of contract in respect of the said agreement and no question as to their claim against the defendant No. 2, even if it is genuine, will be taken as an issue to be adjudicated in the instant suit. Therefore the presence of the applicants in the instant suit are not necessary.

22. The learned senior counsel Mr Kamal-ul-Alam relied upon the case of Zyta Garments Limited vs Union Bank Limited reported in 55 DLR (AD) 56.

23. The learned senior Advocate Mr Kamal-ul Alam next vigorously submitted that the applicants claim against the defendant No. 2 Mr Giasuddin is for the supply of scrap iron. But so long the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' is a floating vessel the same cannot be termed as scrap iron and accordingly no interest to be treated as has been accrued to the applicants through the payment of money to defendant No. 2 for the purpose of purchase scrap iron, which may be obtainable from the floating vessel 'MT Atlanta', unless the vessel is scrapped down and the irons are separated from the said vessel, the applicants will not get any interest in those scrap iron, so long it is attached to the floating vessel 'MT Atlanta'. Even if for the argument sake it is accepted that payment has been made genuinely to the defendant No. 2 Mr Giasuddin, the same will not create any interest in the floating vessel 'MT Atlanta'. Therefore, the applicants are not necessary party in the instant suit on the ground that as they have obtained interest in the vessel and, as such, the question of their so called proportionate title is required to be adjudicated in the instant suit.

24. The learned senior Advocate Mr Kamal-ul-Alam next submitted that the documents and the photocopy of cheques, as have been filed are all false created for the purpose of grabbing the vessel for unlawful gain. The signature, claimed to have been subscribed by the defendant No. 2 on the so called agreement for the purchase of scrap iron from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta', filed by the applicant of the second application, appears to be totally forged one since the admitted signature kept with the plaintiff Bank does not tally at all with the signature as has been claimed to have been subscribed by the defendant No. 2 in the said agreement. Moreover, this agreement has not been signed by the other party Mr Gias Uddin and, as such, this so called agreement can never be treated as an undertaking by the defendant No. 2, since the first page of this so called agreement has not been signed by any party. Therefore, all these documents cannot be taken into consideration, even if for the argument sake it is conceded that the applicants have paid money to the defendant No. 2 for the purpose of purchasing the scrap iron obtainable from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta'.

25. The learned senior counsel Mr Kamal-ul Alam relied upon the case of Aleem Ahmed Ansary vs MV Ashar reported in 1986 PLD Quetta 54 in this respect.

26. The learned senior Advocate Mr Kamal-ul Alam finally submitted that the claim of the applicants do not entitle them to file any Admiralty Suit under the provision of section 3(2) of the Admiralty Court Act 2001 and although a suit, being Admiralty Suit No. 35 of 2016, has been admitted by this court, filed by the applicants and others, yet this court has left the question of maintainability of that suit open and when the court will take the full length hearing of the same the said suit will be dismissed in limine and therefore the suit filed by the applicants in this jurisdiction does not entitled them to be added in the instant suit.

27. The learned senior Advocate Mr Kamal-ul Alam contends that the vessel 'MT Atlanta' was under arrest at the instance of the plaintiff Bank and all the preparation and fixation of date for sell of the said vessel by way of public auction was frustrated due to the instant prayer for addition of party and the plaintiff has face more losses in supplying the expenses of the preparation of the auction sell and, as such, plaintiff is entitled to cost along with the rejection of the instant application.

28. We have heard the learned Advocates and perused the materials on record.

29. This suit has been filed by the plaintiff 'Bank Asia Ltd.' for realization of damage and compensation on the ground that the proprietor of the defendant No. 2, one Md Giasuddin opened L/C through the plaintiff for the purchase and import of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' who upon importing the said vessel failed to repay the L/C amount. The plaintiff Bank being the owner of the vessel under the terms of the L/C is entitled to arrest and sell the vessel for the purpose of realizing the L/C amount and accordingly it has obtained an order of arrest of the defendant No. 1 vessel and all sort of preparation along with fixation of date for holding public auction of the vessel was made, but frustrated due this instant prayer for addition of party.

30. In the instant suit, 3rd party applicants filed application praying for being added as party on the factual ground that the applicants have paid huge amount of money to the said Mr Md Giasuddin, the proprietor of the defendant No. 2, for the purpose of purchasing scrap iron obtainable from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' and, as such, the 3rd party applicants have obtained interest in the defendant No. 1 vessel for which they are necessary party in the instant suit to be added as such.

31. Addition of party is discretionary one. Rule 12 of the Admiralty Rule 1912 has provision as to addition of party in the Admiralty suit which reads as follows;

Admiralty Rules 1912

Rule 12: Intervening in suits in remt.— In a suit in rem any person not named in the writ may intervene and appear on filing an affidavit showing that he is interested in the property under arrest or in the fund in Registry.

<u>32. In order to intervene in a suit in rem, a 3rd party has to establish that it has a subsisting interest either, proprietary or beneficial in the res for which his presence is necessary in the suit else all the question involved suit will not be resolved.</u>

<u>33. Similarly the provision of order 1 rule 10(2) of the Civil Procedure Code 1908 relies on the same principle. But the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 not being applicable in the Admiralty Jurisdiction, as has been decided in the case of Sonali Bank Ltd vs Bangal Liner Ltd., reported in 10 MLR 209 = 10 BLC 148 nevertheless the principle of the said Code as to addition of party may be taken into consideration.</u>

34. The issue of addition of party has been dealt with in order 1 rule 10(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 which is reproduced below for better appreciation;

Civil Procedure Code, 1908

Order I rule 10(2):

The court may, at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such terms as may appear to the court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly jointed, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out, and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added.

<u>35. The aforesaid provision categorically states that in order to "enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved" in the suit, a third party may be added as a defendant in the suit as required not only under principle of order 1 rule 10(2) of the Civil Procedure Code 1908, but also under the provision of rule 12 of the Admiralty rule 1912.</u>

36. In this light we will now examine whether the applicants has fulfilled the requirement of that principle that their presence is necessary in the instant suit for effectual and complete adjudication upon and settled all the question involved in this suit.

37. The plaintiff Bank Asia Limited, a banking company has filed the instant suit against the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' and the defendant No. 2 M/s Al-Madina Enterprise wherein M/s Madian Enterprise was added as a defendant No. 3(a) as parties interested in the vessel 'MT Atlanta'. Later, the said defendant No. 3 was strike down from the plaint on their application. The cause of action which has been stated in the plaint is that the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' was agreed to be sold, by way of memorandum of agreement dated 9th November, 2013, to the defendant No. 2 M/s Al-Madina Enterprise by it's the then owner one M/s Marbird Maritime Inc. Upon the application of the defendant No. 2 the plaintiff opened a L/C in pursuance to a sanction letter dated 18-11-2013 and dated 20-11-2013 for an amount totaling Bd. Taka 59,92,70,000 for the purchase and import of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta', being a navigable old oil tanker, through the L/C being No. 20831302036 dated 19-11-2013 in favour of the said M/s Marbird Maritime Inc. as the beneficiary of the said L/C, which issued the bill of sale dated 20-1-2014 in favour of the plaintiff confirming the receipt of full sell price of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' and transferred the title of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' to the plaintiff on account of the defendant No. 2. Thereafter, the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' reached the Chittagong Port and was beached in the yard situated at Lalbag, South Sitalpur, Sunaichari, Sitakunda, Chittagong. At this juncture it appears to the plaintiff that the defendant No. 2 failed to repay the L/C money to the plaintiff and disappeared from the scene and all attempts to find the defendant No. 2 had failed. The plaintiff being the owner of the vessel has taken all measure to protect the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' in the beach yard by appointing watchmen and by providing substantial sums of money against all expenditure to protect the vessel from destruction of the vessel by the local hood lums, since if the vessel is left uncared for the local hood lums would loot the vessel by cutting the steel plates from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta'. Later, the plaintiff has filed the instant suit for realization of damage and compensation against the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' itself and the defendant No. 2 on the ground that the plaintiff is entitled to realize the L/C amount and the interest at the rate of 18% per annum. Therefore, it appears that the issue to be adjudicated in this suit is the liability of the defendant No. 2 to repay the L/C amount to the plaintiff Bank and the interest on the ground that the plaintiff had imported the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' on account of the defendant No. 2, who is liable to repay the L/C amount along with the outstanding interest and so long the L/C amount is not repaid the L/C opener Bank shall remain the owner of the imported good, herein the defendant No. 1 vessel.

38. It appears that the applicants raised a claim that they have paid huge amount of money to the defendant No. 2 for the purchase of scrap iron to be obtained from the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' and since the proprietor of the defendant No. 2 Mr Giasuddin has failed to comply the undertaking it has made to the applicant for supply of the scrap iron, the applicants are entitled to proceed against the defendant No. 2. This argument prompted us to consider the aspect that if any legal proceeding by way of separate suit is initiated against the defendant No. 2 by the applicants, the issue which will be adjudicated in that suit would be the liability of the defendant No. 2 to the instant applicants on the ground of its failure to supply the negotiated scrap iron. Therefore, the issue involved in the instant suit as stated earlier and the issue to be involved in such a prospective suit in between the defendant No. 2 and the instant applicants are completely different. Therefore, the issue which is involved in the instant Admiralty Suit does not require the applicants to be present in the instant suit for effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settled all the questions involves in the instant suit.

39. It appears that the applicants along with eight others have already initiated an Admiralty Suit being Admiralty Suit No. 35 of 2016 in this jurisdiction, wherein this court has admitted the suit leaving the question of maintainability of the said suit alive. If the instant applicants as plaintiff succeed in that suit their interest will be protected in the said suit and they will not be prejudiced by the adjudication of the instant suit. Because, the applicants claimed that they have the interest in the scrap iron to be supplied by the defendant No. 2 obtainable from the defendant No. 1 vessel. If in that suit the applicants could prove that the defendant No. 2 has failed to supply the scrap iron to them, the relief which has been asked for in the said suit will relieve the applicants. But under no circumstances the interest of the applicants in the scrap iron can be extended to the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta', since the defendant No. 1 vessel is a floating vessel, still navigable, and not turned in to scrap iron. Moreover the title of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta' lies with the plaintiff and not with the defendant No. 2, since the documentary credit which has been allowed to the defendant No. 2 by the plaintiff, provides that the title shall always remain with the financial institution which has allowed the documentary credit till the importer, being the notifying party in the L/C releases the original documents from the L/C opener financial institution upon payment of entire L/C amount along with the stipulated interest. Therefore, up to this stage the defendant No. 2, not being the owner of the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta', has no proprietary title in the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta', although the defendant No. 2 has a beneficial interest in the defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Atlanta', but the same is not transferable to any other party without releasing the original documents from the L/C opener Bank, That being the circumstances the applicants are not required to be present in the instant suit for the purpose of effectual and complete adjudication upon and settle all the questions involved in the instant suit.

40. So far the decision as has been relied upon by the learned Advocate Mr Kamal-ul-Alam as to the privity of contract and the definition of vessel, are not required to be considered at this stage, since on principle the applicants have failed to establish their claim that they are the necessary party in the instant suit on the principle of addition of parties as embodied in rule 12 of the Admiralty Rules 1915 and also in Order 1 rule 10(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908.

41. Therefore, this court finds no merit in the instant application and accordingly the instant two applications are required to be rejected.

42. Accordingly, the instant two applications are rejected.

However, there shall be no order as to cost.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2274 of 2016
lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocate, (with AFM Meshbahuddin, Senior Advocate) instructed by Md. Abdul Hai, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners 
Abdul Baset Majumder, Senior Advocate, (with AJ Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate, Obaidur Rahman Mustafa, Advocate and Masud R. Sobhan, Advocate) instructed by Madhumaloti Chowdhury Barua, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Respondents
parties:
Vice Chancellor, University of Dhaka and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.

case_source: (From the order dated 13-6-2016 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.7550 of 2016)
full_judgment:
Surendra Kumar Sinha CJ: <u>Though this petition arose out of an interim order, the issue involved in the matter has public importance and accordingly we are left with no option other than to dispose of the matter on merit with a view to bring discipline in the admission of students in both public and private medical and Dental Colleges.</u>

2. Writ petitioners who are 153 students of 10 private medical colleges namely; (1) Ashiyan Medical College, Barua, Khilkhet, Dhaka-1215, (2) Dhaka Central International Medical College and Hospital, 2/1 Ring road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka-1207, (3) MH Samorita Medical College, 117 Tejgaon, Love road, Dhaka-1208, (4) City Medical College and Hospital, Aoutpara, Tangail Road, Gazipur Chowrasta, Gazipur-1702, (5) Nightingale Medical College and Hospital, Sarker Market, Asholia Dhaka, (6) Zainul Haque Sikder Womens Medical College and Hospital, Monika Estate, Western Side of Dhanmondi, Dhaka-1209, (7) Care Medical College, 2/1, Iqbal Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka, (8) East-West Medical College, Turag, Dhaka, (9) Tairunnessa Memorial Medical College and Hospital, Konia (Targach) Board Bazar, Gazipur, (10) Aichi Medical College, 35-37, Sector-8, Abdullahpur, Uttara, Dhaka sought judicial review of the decision of Dhaka University refusing to accord registration and issue admit cards for the 1st professional MBBS examination for the academic session 2014-2015 to be unlawful and a direction be given to issue such cards enabling them to appear in the examination.

<u>3. Substance of their claim is that the government issued a Circular for admission into MBBS/BDS courses in 2011 (Nitimala of 2011) for the academic session 2012-2013. Under the said Nitimala 2011 a student would be eligible to get admission who scored highest marks out of 200 marks and the basis of selection of an eligible student is that out of 200 marks, 100 marks to be calculated on the basis of GPA score in SSC and HSC and 100 marks in written test. Students who secured top list on merit would be eligible for admission in the academic session. It was decided that students scoring 120 marks out of 200 marks in the merit list would be admitted. Challenging the said decision Bangladesh Private Medical College Association (BPMCA) filed Writ Petition No.1337 of 2014. A Division Bench of the High ade the rule absolute. Another writ petition was also filed by 52 students of the aforesaid 10 private medical colleges being Writ Petition No.669 of 2015 on the same issue and the rule was also made absolute. In pursuance of the latter judgment, the students were admitted to the aforesaid 10 Medical Colleges. Against the judgment passed in writ petition No. 1337 of 2014 the government preferred CA 5 No.147 of 2015 and two other leave petitions but that appeal and those petitions were dismissed. In pursuance of the said judgment, the offices of the writ respondent No.2, the principals of the Medical Colleges forwarded the applications for registration of the names of the writ petitioners but the Registrar, Dhaka University refused to register their names and thereupon the Controller of Examinations, Dhaka University published the time table for the examination. The writ petitioners made repeated request to get their names registered but the University authority did not allow registration to them nor accorded permission to face the first year professional MBBS examination scheduled to start on 2nd May, 2016.</u>

4. A Division Bench of the High Court Division passed the impugned order in following terms:

"The respondents (writ respondents) are directed to issue Registration Card for the forthcoming 1st professional MBBS Examination of the petitioners within 72 hours and allow them to appear in the forthcoming examination 1st professional Examination".

5. Against the said order the university authority moved this court and obtained an order of stay. From the averments it is clear that the writ petitioners said to have been admitted to the aforesaid 10 private medical colleges in pursuance of the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.669 of 2015 and that the college authorities sent their applications for registration in pursuance of the judgment of this court in Civil Appeal No.147 of 2015. It is on record that these private medical colleges admitted the students for the academic sessions 2013-2014 and 2014-2015 after securing judgments from the High Court Division. It is also pertinent to note here that though the first writ petition was filed by BPMCA, the second writ petition was filed by the students of those private medical colleges and this time also the students of the said private medical colleges moved the writ petition. They claimed that in pursuance of the judgment of the High Court Division the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare directed to comply with the judgment of the court and that the principals of the medical colleges forwarded their applications for according registration. Apparently the students had no responsibility in the matter of registration of their names with the Dhaka University. It is the college authorities which had taken the responsibility and obligation to get their students' registration with Dhaka University, but the college authorities this time tacitly refrained from seeking judicial review of the decision taken by Dhaka University authority though they sent the students' applications after performing formalities as their regular students. It may be said that the college authorities utilized the sentiments of the students to secure an order from the High Court Division to get their names registered although it was none of their business to apply for registration and therefore, they are not legally entitled to seek judicial review in this regard.

6. In course of hearing of the matter, this court meticulously perused the pleadings made in previous two writ petitions, the judgments and the pleadings of the present writ petition, and it led to believe that this time the college authorities played trick to utilize the sympathy of the students and secured the interim order through them. Accordingly this court issued show cause notices upon them to explain why they should not be proceeded against by imposing penalty for violation of the decisions of the government under memos dated 1st July, 2014 and 14 December, 2014 and the University under memo dated 19 October, 2014 for admitting 153 students in their medical colleges for the academic session 2014-2015. They showed cause and stated that they admitted the students in pursuance of the decisions of the High Court Division; that the University authority was corum-non-judice in introducing the cut-off mark; that the colleges did not give admission to any students who did not secure 40 marks in the written examination and that it was only after the judgment passed in Writ Petition No.669 of 2015, they admitted the students. So they took similar stand with the students.

7. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner submitted that the High Court Division fell in an error in making the interim direction upon Dhaka University ignoring the decisions taken by the University and the government. In this connection he has drawn our attention to the decisions taken by the authorities regarding the conditions attached for getting admission of the students in the academic session 2014-2015. The first decision relied upon is a resolution headed by the Minister, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in which the representatives of the Private Medical Colleges, Dean of Medical Faculty, Dhaka University, General Secretary, Bangladesh Medical Association, Secretary BPMCA were present. The secretary of the said association requested to fix up the amount of money to be spent by a student of private medical college in the similar manner a student of government medical colleges spends in MBBS/BDS courses. In the said meeting the question of cut-off mark and criteria for admission for the academic session 2014-2015 were discussed in which one representative from a private medical college proposed that the minimum score of 120 marks should be fixed for admission. The Registrar, Dhaka University proposed that the students must score 40 marks in written examination in the similar manner the students of first year honours courses are admitted. After a threadbare discussion, it was resolved amongst others that—

“এমবিবিএস/বিডিএস কোর্স ভর্তি পরীক্ষায় ২০০ এর মধ্যে ১২০ নম্বর প্রাপ্ত ছাত্র/ছাত্রীদের ভর্তি করা যাবে এবং উক্ত ছাত্র/ছা্ত্রীদের ভর্তি করা যাবে এবং উক্ত ছাত্র/ছাত্রীদের লিখিত পরীক্ষায় ৪০ নম্বর পেতে হবে।” It was decided that a student would be eligible to get admission in the academic session scoring 120 marks and must secure 40 marks in written examination out of 100 marks.

8. Dhaka University authority accordingly issued a Circular in pursuance of Dean Committee's decision taken on 1st October, 2014, prescribing the criteria for admission of students under the University in respect of government medical colleges and private dental/medical colleges for the academic session 2014-2015. The relevant portion is quoted below:

“স্বাস্থ্য ও পরিবার কল্যাণ মন্ত্রণালয়ের সিদ্ধান্ত অনুযায়ী ২০১৪-২০১৫ শিক্ষাবর্ষে ১ম বর্ষ এমবিবিএস ও বিডিএ.স কোর্সে ভর্তি পরীক্ষার যোগ্যতা সম্পন্ন ভর্তিচ্ছু ছাত্র/ছাত্রীকে পরীক্ষায় ১০০ নম্বরের মধ্যে ৪০ নম্বর পেতে হবে। এর নীচে প্রাপ্ত কোন ছাত্র/ছাত্রীদের ভর্তি করা যাবে না।

বিগত ২০১৩-২০১৪ শিক্ষাবর্ষে সেই শিক্ষাবর্ষের সিদ্ধান্ত অনুযায়ী মেধাস্কোর ১২০ এর নীচে নম্বর প্রাপ্ত কোন ছাত্র/ছাত্রীকে নিয়ম বহির্ভুতভাবে ভর্তি করা হলে তাদেরকে রেজিষ্ট্রেশন দেয়া হবে না মর্মে কলেজ কর্তৃপক্ষকে জানিয়ে দেয়া হোক।” It clearly directed that the students must score 40 written marks out of 100 and that any student scoring below the said mark would not be eligible for admission. It was pointed out that the said decision should be intimated to all concerned. There was no ambiguity in the decision prohibiting the medical colleges not to admit students who could not secure 40 marks in the written examination.

9. Subsequently the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare had taken another resolution and in the said meeting also the representatives of all medical colleges both private and public throughout the country had attended. It was unanimously decided prescribing the criteria for admission in the first year MBBS course for the academic session 2014-2015. It was directed that the students must score 40 written marks for admission. The decision is as under:

“২০১৪-২০১৫ শিক্ষাবর্ষে এমবিবিএস/বিডিএস কোর্স��� ছাত্র/ছাত্রী ভর্তি কমিটির ১-৭-২০১৪ তারিখের সভায় ভর্তি পরীক্ষায় ২০০ এর মধ্যে ১২০ নম্বর প্রাপ্ত ছাত্র/ছাত্রীদের ভর্তি করা যাবে এবং উক্ত ছাত্র/ছাত্রীদের লিখিত পরীক্ষায় নূন্যতম ৪০ নম্বর পেতে হবে মর্মে গৃহীত সিদ্ধান্তটি বহাল থাকবে”. It was said that out of 200 marks, the students who scored 120 marks could be eligible for admission, but the students must also score 40 written marks out of 100 marks.

10. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, submitted that these decisions of the authorities are binding upon the aforesaid private medical colleges and the said colleges cannot take exception on the doctrine of estoppel, inasmuch as, the decision was taken in their presence and within their knowledge, and that they had admitted the students defying the decisions of the concerned authorities. He argued that these medical colleges admitted the students for deriving monetary gains without considering the future of the students. They have no sympathy towards the students and they are not also at all concerned about the improvement in the medical education. The organizers set up colleges with the motive of profit taking the medical education as business. We find force in the contention of the learned counsel.

11. Mr. Sobhan, learned counsel appearing for the private medical colleges reiterated the statements made in reply to the show cause notice and banks upon the judgments as mentioned above. According to him the decision for admission was taken in pursuance of the judgment of the High Court Division in writ petition No. 669 of 2015. This submission nakedly focused the motive of those colleges that they utilized the students in the earlier writ petition and this time also, they defying the decisions of the authorities admitted the students.

12. In Writ Petition No.1337 of 2014, though the memos dated 23rd September, 2013 and 5th November, 2013 were challenged, in the first memo issued by the government it was resolved that the students could be admitted to in the academic session 2012-2013 who secured 120 marks out of 200 marks and in the latter memo issued by the Directorate of Health services, a direction was given prescribing the guidelines for admission of the students in the academic session 2013-2014. In the present writ petition the question is whether the medical colleges legally admitted the students defying the decisions given by the authorities prescribing the guide line that no student could be admitted without securing 40 marks in written examination out of 100 marks for the academic year 2014-2015. The writ petitioner in the first petition sought a declaration that the increase of the minimum cut-off mark from 110 to 120 out of total 200 marks was without lawful authority. It is contended by Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali appearing for the students that in Writ Petition No.669 of 2015, the question of scoring marks was an issue. The submission is devoid of substance, inasmuch as, in the said writ petition the Nitimala 2011 was challenged. The prayer made in the writ petition was "(i) Nitimal 2011" as of Annexure-"A" published should not declared as having been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect".

13. The students claimed that in pursuance of the said judgment passed in writ petition No.669 of 2015, the college authorities admitted them but the University authority did not accord registration of their names. In Writ Petition No.1337 of 2014 the High Court Division discussed in detail the criteria for admission for the academic session 2013-2014. In pursuance of the Nitimala 2011, the Circular dated 4-12-2012 was issued with regard to admission of students in MBBS/BDS courses in medical colleges clearly stipulating that "the cut-off marks for admission in to MBBS/BDS courses would be 110 and 105 respectively (annexure-D) and an advertisement was published pursuant to the said Nitimala (annexure-C) and Circular (annexure-D)'. In the Nitimala nothing was stipulated about the cut-off mark. There was direction for holding centralized admission test in which a merit list would be prepared on the basis of marks to be scored by students out of 200 marks. It was directed that100 marks to be calculated on the basis of GPA score and 100 marks on the basis of written test and that students scoring top of the merit list would get opportunity for admission to government medical colleges and the rest eligible students from the merit list would get the opportunity in private medical colleges. However, in memo dated 4-12-2012, the Health and Family Welfare Ministry issued guidelines for admission of students prescribing cut-off mark and pursuant to that an advertisement was published on 31-8-2013 and the new cut-off mark had been introduced. It was held in writ petition No.669 of 2015 that the writ respondents were acting at their own caprice and whims without bothering to adhere to their own Nitimala, and apart from that, they were not even obliging their own letter dated 7-1-2014.

14. This court in Civil Appeal No.147 of 2015 held as under:

"Admittedly, the impugned decision-raising the minimum "cut-off' mark from110 to 120 was taken by a committee headed by the respondent No.1 and not by the Council, namely, Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (MBDC) which has been formed as per law. Section 5 of this Act shows that this Council (BMDC) is empowered to deal with almost all the matters relating to medical and Dental Institutions including framing of guidelines etc. for admission to MBB Sand BDS courses. The setting of "cut-off' mark for being eligible for admission to MBBS and BDS courses falls within these powers of BMDC and as such the BMDC only is empowered to fix or set the minimum "cut-off' mark for being eligible for admission to these courses. Admittedly, the impugned decision raising the "cut-off' mark from 110 to 120 was not taken by this BMDC, rather it was taken by the respondent No.1 and some other persons."

15. So, the issue in that case was regarding raising of the minimum cut-off mark from 110-105 to 120-110 respectively after issuance of admission circular for the academic session 2013-2014.

16. In writ petition No.669 of 2015 in Paragraph 10 it was stated that the concerned Ministry issued a circular on 15-7-2014, annexure-F, wherein in Paragraph 11(ga) it directed that the students must score 40 marks in the written examination besides scoring 120 out of 200 marks. Though this letter was annexed, the scoring 40 marks in the written examination was not an issue and the court did not give any opinion in this regard. The High Court Division declared that the said circular setting up 120 marks as the should criteria for passing the test for admission into MBBS/BDS courses in Government/Private Medical/Dental Colleges for 2014-2015 academic session was illegal.

17. Now the question is whether the colleges were justified in admitting the students in pursuance of the judgment passed in writ petition No. 669 of 2015. Article 4 of the Dhaka University Order, 1973 provides that the University may exercise powers to affiliate colleges; to prescribe courses of studies to be conducted by the University or its affiliated colleges; to hold examinations and to grant and confer certificate, diplomas, degree set Article 25 prescribes the powers of Academic Council. It said that 'the Council shall subject to the provision of the Order, Statutes and the University Ordinances, have the control and general supervision over, and be responsible for maintenance of standards of instruction, education and examination within the University and shall exercise such other powers as may be conferred or imposed upon it by the statutes. It shall have the right to advise the Syndicate oral academic matters. Article 39 authorises the University to promulgate Statutes as set out in the schedule. Article 27 deals with the Faculties. Clause (3) of Article 27 provides that the Faculties shall be advisory bodies and their decision shall be submitted to the syndicate through Academic Council for implementation. Section 5 of the First Statute empowers the Academic Council to perform the following acts:

"(a) to make regulations for and to award in accordance with such Regulations, Fellowships, Scholarships, Exhibitions, bursaries, medals and other rewards;

(b) ------------------------------

(c) ------------------------------

(d) to formulate, modify or revise, subject to the control of the syndicate, schemes for the constitution or reconstitution of Faculties and for the assignment of subjects to such Faculties."

18. There are several Faculties prescribed in section 6, in addition to Article 27(1) of the order and section 9 deals with the Faculty of Medicine. Section 16 prescribes the powers of the Faculty, such as—

(a) to constitute Committees of Courses and Studies; (b) to recommend to the Academic Council, after consulting the Committees of Courses and Studies, the names of the examiners in subjects assigned to the Faculty. Section 17 deals with the Deans wherein sub-section (I) provides:—

“The Dean of each faculty shall be the executive officer of the Faulty and shall preside at its meetings ------------”

19. Section 43 is relevant for our consideration which provides for Administration of Departments. Sub-section (3) provides that the Academic Committee shall deal with—

(a) Admission of students;

(b) Syllabuses;

(c) Examinations;

(d) Teaching in the department;

(e) Co-curricular activities of the students in the department.

20. Therefore, there is no gain saying that the Dean of each Faculty is the Chief Executive Officer rather the Academic Committee shall deal with admission of students. In exercise of that power, the Deans Committee issued the guidelines for admission of the students in Medical Colleges for the academic session 2014-2015 and one of those criteria was that the students must score 40 marks in written examination out of 100 marks.

21. The Medical and Dental Council Ain, 2010 empowers the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council to recognize the competency of the education to be given by the medical and dental institutions; to recognize the students obtaining degrees from other medical and dental colleges outside Bangladesh; to settle the standard courses of the degrees and post degree courses and to settle the admission of students in degree and post degree courses in medical and dental colleges. Though this Ain was promulgated in 2010, no Rules or Guidelines or Regulations for admission of students have been formulated as yet by the Council. Even if it is assumed that the Council has formulated Guidelines, none of the parties has produced any such Guidelines in that regard. The object of promulgating the Ain is to monitor the standard of medical education and to recognise the medical and dental graduates, post graduates both from home and abroad but it retains no power to confer degree to the students. It has the power to recognise the medical colleges in accordance with section 12. There is a provision for registration of the students of recognized institutions, but the writ petitioners sought their registration with Dhaka University from which it may be inferred that the Ain has not been implemented in full swing. Even if the Council has power to regulate the standard of education to be given by the medical colleges, it can't compel the University to relax the criteria for admission of students. The Council is at an elementary stage. There is no doubt that the Act of 2010 has force of law, but the admission criteria and other related matters for maintaining the standard education of the medical students are regulated by the University and that is why the students sought their registration with Dhaka University.

<u>22. More so, this Ain will not prevail over the University Statutes since the medical and dental students are obtaining degrees and post degree certificates from Dhaka University. The University Statutes have force of law and on the strength of those Statutes; the University regulates the criteria for admission of medical students' syllabus. There is no doubt that the Ain of 2010 was promulgated to cover the field of medical education and to oversee standard of medical education providing by the public and private medical colleges. The Medical Council has power not to recognise a degree certificate issued by any public or private University in or outside Bangladesh. It can also suggest the public Universities to incorporate a particular course or subject for degree or post degree courses, and if the Universities do not follow its advice, it may withhold recognition of the students obtaining certificates by the said Universities. Yet it cannot compel Dhaka University to relax the guide lines for admission into MBBS course since this University is the sole authority to issue medical graduation certificates within its jurisdiction.</u>

23. Since the Writ Petitioners seek direction upon Dhaka University to get their name registered for 1st year MBBS examination admit cards, they must satisfy the criteria and guidelines given by the University authority because of the fact that unless it issues graduation certificates, they will not be recognized as graduates by the Council-constituted under Ain of 2010. The power to co-ordinate standards of education lies with the Parliament. The Parliament has power to prevent disparity of standard of education in different Universities by promulgating law but this does not mean that the Parliament can interfere in the internal administration of the university.

<u>24. A decision is flawed if it is illegal and if the authority contravenes or exceeds the terms of the power which authorises the making of the decision, judicial review is available against such decision. The task for a court of law in assessing whether a decision is illegal is essentially one of construing the content and scope of the instrument conferring the duty or power upon decision maker. The court is to determine whether an authority has made an error of law in making the decision. There is number of issues that arise in public law that make the court's task more complex. This task is made easier where the purpose is clearly defined, or where the considerations which the body must take into account in arriving at its decision are clearly spelled out. In such cases the court requires the decision-maker to take into account the specified considerations and ignore the irrelevant.</u>

25. The students were admitted by the concerned colleges in pursuance of the judgment passed in Writ Petition No.669 of 2015. Though the High Court Division discussed the minutes of the resolution of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (annexure-F), the issue of scoring 40 written marks was not an issue in the writ petition. The High Court Division declared that `the admission procedure for MBBS/BDS courses for all Medical Colleges, Government or Private be done by respondent No.5, the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council in accordance with the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council Act and for ensuing year i.e. 2014-2015 admission of MBBS/BDS students be done 'by ignoring the threshold cut-off marks'.

<u>26. The concerned Ministry and Dhaka University specifically directed that the students must score 40 marks out of 100 in the written examination for the academic session 2014-2015. The aforesaid 10 colleges admitted the students defying that direction and instead of challenging the decision taken by the authorities, utilized the sentiments of the students in the High Court Division. The colleges were under obligation to get the students registered with Dhaka University following the guidelines given by it. These colleges in the previous academic session also admitted the students by securing a judgment from the High Court Division through the students and in the next academic session as well, they admitted the students in violation of the decisions of the government and the University. There are some issues which are inherently unsuited for judicial determination. Even if a matter falls within the jurisdiction of administrative authority and is justifiable, there are a good number of reasons why the court may properly exercise its discretion to refuse to consider a claim for judicial review. The decision involving policy utilitarian calculation of the public good such decisions about the levels of taxation or public expenditure are constitutionally in the realm of legislature and not judicially reviewable. It is settled that the court will not interfere with policy decision merely because it feels that another policy decision could have been fairer or wiser or more scientific or logical [Balco Employees Union vs India, 2002 (2) SCC 3330]. This court accepted the views taken in that case and we find no cogent reason to differ from the same. Same principle is applicable in case of admission of students, inasmuch as, it is the policy decision of the University authority.</u>

<u>27. The High Court Division cannot regulate the criteria for the admission of students in MBBS/BDS courses. The authority which is authorized by law to deal with a subject should be allowed to perform its duty and responsibility in accordance with laws governing that subject. This exercise of powers by the High Court Division may be taken as usurpation of power not sanctioned by law. Every organ of the State should be allowed to perform its onerous responsibility in accordance with their respective laws. If the court interferes with their internal administration and the eligibility of admission of students in any University, this will tantamount to exercise of a power not vested in law. The court should refrain itself from interfering with the internal administration of an authority if such authority does not contravene the law and it can interfere only in those cases where there is infraction of law in taking decision affecting the right of a citizen. The court shall always keep in mind while exercising its power of judicial review that it has not transgressed the jurisdiction in any authority transacting its business.</u>

28. The Medical Colleges mentioned above utterly violated the Statutes of Dhaka University and by defying its guidelines admitted the students and thereby they have gambled with the students for their personal gains. Their conduct is deprecated. They have violated laws repeatedly and thus, unless they are dealt with severely, they would recur similar violation in future. This petition is disposed of with the above observations. This short order shall form part of this judgment.

End.
