full_judgment:
Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J: This petition for leave to appeal has been filed against the judgment and decree dated the 4th day of June, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No.328 of 1994 allowing the same.

2. Facts necessary for disposal of this petition are that respondent Nos. 1-4 as plaintiffs filed Other Class Suit No: 167 of 1990 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chittagong for the following reliefs:

"ক) বাদীগণ  ১৬-১-৭৯, ১৮-১-৭৮ ইংরেজি তারিখের  চট্টগ্রাম  সদর সাব  রেজিস্ট্রি অফিসের যথাক্রমে ৫৫৮,৬৬৫, ৬৬৬ ও ৭৬৩ নং কবলামূলে মৃত হাজী ইমাম শরীফ হইতে তপশীল বর্ণিত জমি খরিদ করিয়া তাহাতে আইনঃ স্বত্বঅর্জন করিয়াছি ঘোষণা মর্মে উক্ত জমিতে তাহাদের স্থিরতরের ডিক্রী দেওয়ার আদেশ হয়।

খ) ৩নং বিবাদী ও  মৃত হাজী ইমাম শরীফ এর মধ্যে কথিতসম্পাদিত রেজিস্ট্রিকৃত ৩০-১-৭৩ ইংরেজি সনের ৬ ও ৭ নং বণ্টননামা দলিল বেআইনী যোগাযোগী, পণ্ড, অকার্যকর এবং তৎমূলে তপশীল বর্ণিত জমিতে বাদীগণের স্বত্বের কোন ব্যাঘাত হয় নাই এবং তদ্বারা ৩নং বিবাদী কোন রকম স্বত্বদখল অর্জন করেন নাই মর্মে ডিক্রী দেওয়ার আদেশ হয়।

গ) ১ ও ২ বিবাদীর চট্টগ্রাম ১নং সাব জজ আদালতের ১৯৮৮ সনের ৮০ নং মামলায় ৩ নং বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধেডিক্রীমূলে তফশীল বর্ণিত জমিতে বাদীগণের স্বত্ব দখলেরকোন হানি হয় নাই মর্মে ডিক্রী দেওয়ার আজ্ঞা হয়।

ঘ) চিরস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার দ্বারা বিবাদীগণকে তপশীল বর্ণিতজমিতে বাদীগণের দখলে কোন রুপ হস্তক্ষেপ ও ব্যাঘাত সৃষ্টি না করার জন্য নিষেধাজ্ঞার ডিক্রী দেওয়ার আজ্ঞা হয়।

ঙ) অত্র মামলা চলকালীন সময়ে বাদীগণকে গায়ের জোরেবাদীগণকে তপশীল বর্ণিত জমি বা ইহার কোন অংশ হইতে বে-দখল করিলে তাহার দখল পুনরুদ্ধারের ডিক্রী দেওয়ার আদেশ হয়।

চ) মামলার খরচ প্রতিদ্বন্দ্বিতাকারি বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রী দেওয়ার আদেশ হয়।

ছ) বাদীগণ অন্য যে, যে প্রতিকার আইনঃ পাইতে পারেন তাহা ডিক্রী দেওয়ার আদেশ হয়।

"3. The suit was contested by defendant Nos.1 and 2 by filing written statement. Though defendant Nos. 4 and 5 filed written statement, they did not contest the suit ultimately.

4. The trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 12-6-1994 dismissed the suit. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the plaintiffs filed First Appeal No. 328 of 1994 before the High Court Division. A Division Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and decree allowed the appeal and sent the suit back to the trial Court for fresh trial with the direction upon it to proceed with the suit after service of summons upon defendant No.3 on the finding, inter alia, that the order sheets showed that summons of the suit was not served upon the defendant. The High Court Division further held that as summons of the suit was not served upon defendant No; 3, the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court was a nullity. The High Court Division did not at all enter into the merit, of the case of the plaintiffs, though the appeal was filed by them against the judgment and decree of the trial Court dismissing the suit.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the High Court Division, the heirs of defendant No. 3 have filed this petition for leave to appeal as he died in the meantime.

<u>6. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Counsel, for the petitioners submits that the plaintiffs having felt aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial Court dismissing the suit, preferred the first appeal in question, so the High Court Division as the last Court of fact was obliged to see whether the trial Court committed any error factually and legally in dismissing the suit, but it without directing its attention in that respect made out a third case that as summons of the suit was not served upon defendant No.3, the judgment and decree passed in the suit was a nullity. He further submits that when defendant No.3 appeared in the first appeal and made no compliant as to the non-service of summons upon him, the High Court Division ought not to have sent the suit to the trial Court for service of summons of the suit afresh upon him and then to proceed with the suit and it should have disposed of the appeal on merit. The impugned judgment and decree calls for interference by this Court.</u>

7. Mr Sheikh Mohammad Morshed, learned Advocate who entered caveat on behalf of the plaintiff-respondents on the other hand, supported the impugned judgment and decree. He submits that as summons of the suit was not served upon defendant No.3, the. hearing of the suit should not have commenced, the High Court Division rightly remanded the suit to the trial Court and no interference is called for with the impugned judgment and decree.

<u>8. As stated earlier, the plaintiffs' suit was dismissed and the appeal was filed by them. Let us see what the points were taken before the High Court Division on behalf of the appellants. In the memorandum of appeal as many as 16(sixteen) grounds were taken and not a single ground was taken as to the non-service of summons upon defendant No.3 for which the proceedings of the suit could be said to be illegal and the judgment and decree passed therein a nullity. At the time of hearing the appeal, no such point was also urged either by the learned Advocate for the appellants or by the learned Advocates for the defendant- respondents (besides respondent No.3, respondent No. 2 also contested the appeal). The submission made by the learned Advocate for the appellants as noted in the impugned judgment and decree were as under:</u>

<u>"Mr SK Md Morshed, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant placed the ground taken by him in the memo of appeal, and thereafter submitted that the plaintiff’s proved his (sic, it would be their) case by oral and documentary evidence, but the trial court without appreciating the evidence on record, exhibited documents and plaintiff's case dismissed the suit. He draws our attention to the ground No. 14, and submits that the suit was wrongly dismissed on the finding that it was bad for defect of parties. He submits that the heirs of the original owners, as well as defendant No.3, were parties in the suit, and there being no case that any other person has had got any interest in the suit land, there is no defect of parties in the suit. He submits that the defendant No.3, was served with summons but did not appear in the suit and the suit was accordingly taken up for ex-parte hearing, and draws our attention to the order sheet of the court below and submits that the plaintiffs of the suit submitted the requisites for the service of summons on the defendant and the summons were issued by registered post, and also by process server, by the order dated 10-11-1990 and it was fixed for the return of service, thereafter on 2-2-1991. He referring to the report of the process server from the LC record submits that the summons was issued against the defendant No.3 and it was served by hanging and there is report of the process server to that effect. Beside this, the summons were also served under registered post, and that the presumption in such event is, that the summon was duly served and the trial Court on the failure of the defendant No.3 in appearing in the suit proceeded with the suit against the defendant No.3 for ex parte disposal, and there was no wrong committed by the trial Court in proceeding of the suit against the defendant No.3 ex-parte. The defendant being served with the process duly did not appear in the suit, and consequently it was decided against defendant No. 3 ex-parte. The defendant No.3 is the respondent No.3, in the appeal, and he on receipt of the notice of the appeal entered appearance in the appeal by engaging learned Advocate."</u>

9. So, from the submissions made before the High Court Division on behalf of the appellants, it is rather clear that they insisted very much that summons of the suit was served upon defendant No.3, in both ways, by the process server as well as by registered post.

10. Interestingly, though the High Court Division found that summons of the suit was not served upon defendant No.3, but defendant No.3 who was respondent No.3 in the appeal appeared through his lawyer, Mr Md Asadullah and did not make any complaint or grievance about non-service of summons of the suit upon him. Rather his learned Advocate made a candid submission as noted in the impugned judgment to the effect "appearing for the respondent no. 3 admitted in his oral submission that the defendant no. 3 had knowledge about the suit, but he did not contest the suit. But, he being served with notice in the appeal, appeared to contest the appeal and he will make submissions on the law point for the respondent, defendant No.3, in the suit. He made submission about his entitlement to submit on the law point in the appeal, and he next submits that the appeal is the continuation of the suit, though, the defendant opted not to contest the suit, but now, the suit having been dismissed by judgment and decree impugned in the appeal, he submits, that the plaint of the suit is not maintainable, and the trial Court rightly dismissed the suit. "The very submission of the learned Advocate for respondent No.3 quoted above, prima facie shows that summons of the suit was served upon him, but he chose not to appear in the suit and contest the same. But that does not mean that defendant No. 3 cannot contest the appeal. He has every right to contest the appeal regarding the factual aspect of the case as well as the legal aspect which followed from the evidence on record. In the Code of Civil procedure -aspect which followed from the evidence on record (the Code), there is no provision that a defendant, who did not appear in the suit in spite of service of summons upon him and did not file any written statement, cannot contest an appeal filed against the decree passed in a suit on the evidence on record.

<u>11. In the context, it may be stated that even a third party can file an appeal in case he is affected by a decree passed in a suit. But unfortunately, the High Court Division did not accept the said submission of the learned Advocate for defendant No.3-respondent on the view "As we have found from the record that the summons was not served on the defendant No.3 and that the defendant did not enter in the suit the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondent No.3 in the appeal that the defendant no.3 opted not to contest the suit is not tenable in the facts on record, which is against the scheme of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendant being served with the process of summons in the suit, or having knowledge of the suit is to enter appearance in the suit, and answer the plaint, should be in attendance in the Court house in person or by his pleader. Under the Rule requires the attendance of the defendant on being served with summons. In this case, the submission of learned Advocate that the defendant opted not to contest in the suit is not contemplated in the Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure the consequence of his non appearance in the suit has to be followed."</u>

<u>12. In taking the above view, the High Court Division totally failed to consider the legal position that in Order IX, rules 6( 1 )(a) and 11 of the Code, the consequences of non-appearance of a defendant on the date fixed for hearing the suit, in case summons was served upon him, have been clearly spelt out; the consequence is that the suit would be heard ex-parte against the defaulting defendant. That actually happened in the instant case. Defendant Nos. I and 2, 4 and 5 appeared in the suit and filed separate written statements. As defendant Nos. 4 and 5 did not contest the suit ultimately, the suit was dismissed on contest against defendant Nos.1 and 2 and ex-parte against the other defendants including defendant No.3. But the High Court Division without considering the provisions of rules 6(1 )(a) and 11 of Order IX of the Code considered rule 1 of Order IX only and thus fell in an error in refusing the learned Advocate for defendant-respondent No.3 in making submission on the point of law.</u>

13. The High Court Division was not also factually correct in finding that summons of the suit was not served upon defendant No.3, as report of the process server clearly showed that summons of the suit was served upon defendant No.3 by hanging and he gave report to that effect. Merely because the fact of service of summons upon defendant No.3 was not recorded in the order sheet, it may be through inadvertence which did not make the report of the process server as regards service of summons upon defendant No.3 ineffective or nonest. Moreso, it further appears that summons of the suit was also sent to defendant No.3 by registered post in compliance with the provisions of Order V, rule 19B of the Code. When attention of Mr. Morshed was drawn to the fact that he did not make any submission before the High Court Division as to the non-service of summons upon defendant No.3, rather he insisted that summons of the suit was served upon him, he submitted that even if no submission was made, the Appellate Court was under an obligation to see the entire record and be satisfied whether summons of the suit were served upon the defendants before the commencement of the trial of the suit. We failed to understand any logic behind the said submission of Mr Morshed. The Code enjoins that the plaintiffs are to take necessary step in the suit for service of summons upon the defendants and the objection, as to the non-service of notice, if any, can be taken only by the defendant(s). Mr Morshed himself made submission before the High Court Division by pointing out from the lower Court's record that there was report of the process server with the record that he served summons upon defendant No. 3 as per provision of rules 17-19 of the Code, he could not make a reverse submission before this Court just to support the impugned judgment and decree. And such attempt shows that somehow the plaintiffs were interested to get a fresh trial of the suit by the trial Court to fill up the lacuna in their case as pointed out by the trial Court in its judgment and decree. Further defendant No.3 appeared before the High Court Division in the appeal and his learned Advocate made the submission that the defendant had knowledge about the suit, but he opted not to appear in the suit and wanted to contest the appeal on the point of law through his learned Advocate which, in effect, proved that defendant No. 3 accepted the factual position that summons of the suit was duly served upon him; the question of service of summons upon the defendant afresh did not arise at all.

<u>14. In the context, it may be stated that Mr. Mustafa Neaz Mohammad, learned Advocate for respondent No.2 also made submission that summons of the suit was duly served upon defendant No.3. He further submitted that the trial Court rightly dismissed the suit and there was no illegality in the judgment and decree of the dismissal. Therefore, the High Court Division was totally wrong in sending the suit on remand to the trial Court for hearing the same afresh after service of summons upon defendant No.3. It further appears that the plaintiffs and defendant Nos.1 and 2 adduced evidence both oral and documentary in support of their respective case and the trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit, the plaintiff filed the appeal against such dismissal, so it was incumbent upon the High Court Division as the last Court of fact to see whether the trial Court was correct in dismissing the suit, instead it sent the suit on remand to the trial Court on a point which was never urged by any of the parties in the appeal. In passing the impugned judgment and decree, the High Court Division also failed to consider the legal proposition that even a suit is heard ex parte. the plaintiff cannot get a walk over and he has to prove his own case.</u>

15. For the discussions made above, the impugned judgment and decree cannot be sustained in law.

<u>16. Be that as it may, since the High Court Division did not enter into the merit of the appeal and sent the suit on remand to the trial Court for fresh hearing on the erroneous view of the facts and the law as pointed out hereinbefore and we have heard both the parties, we consider it proper to send the appeal back to the High Court Division for hearing the same afresh and dispose I of the same in accordance with law on the evidence on record. Accordingly, this petition is disposed of in the following terms:</u>

<u>The impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division is set aside. The appeal is sent back to the High Court Division for hearing afresh and dispose of the same in accordance with law on the evidence on record. The first appeal shall be heard and disposed of by the Bench presided over by Nozrul Islam Chowdhury, J. within 2(two) months from the date of receipt of this judgment.</u>

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 22-23 of 2011
lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate with Probir Neogi, Advocate instructed by Md Nawab Ali.Advocate- on-Record ----- For the Petitioner (In both the cases) 
PC Guha, Advocate instructed by Purabi Saha, Advocate-an-Record ----- For the Respondents (In both the cases).
parties:
Nurul Hoq Bhuiyan ------ Petitioner
VS
Momtazul Isalm and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 8-11-2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1394 of 2008 along with Civil Revision No. 2821 of 2008.)
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J: Both these Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal, at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant, are directed against the judgment and order dated 8-11-2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1394 of 2008 along with Civil Revision No. 2821 of 2008.

<u>2. The relevant facts necessary for disposal of these Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal are as follows:</u>

<u>The present petitioner along with three others instituted Title Suit No 705 of 2005 in the 3rd Court of Joint District Judge. Comilla against the opposite parties for partition of the suit land described in schedule to the plaint. The case of the plaintiff, in short, was that the suit land originally belonged to Alimuddin Bhuiyan-who died leaving 5 sons, namely, Abbas Ali Bhuiyan, Amir Uddin Bhuiyan, Hossain Uddin Bhuiyan, Ali Azam and Abdul Aziz Bhuiyan by his 1st wife and other 2 sons, namely, Ibrahim Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan by his 2nd wife. Alimuddin Bhuiyan during his life time distributed his property amongst the aforesaid 7 sons by a registered deed of gift dated 27-10-1911. As per said deed of gift Amir Uddin Bhuiyan got 9.83 acres of land. Amir Uddin Bhuiyan died leaving defendant Nos. 2-15 as his heirs and successors. Abbas Ali Bhuiyan got 9.45 acres of land who subsequently died leaving defendant Nos. 16-26 as his heirs and successive heirs. Hossain Uddin Bhuiyan got 8.664/9 the acres of land and he died leaving defendant Nos. 27-35 as his heirs and successors. Ali Azam Bhuiyan got 9.144/9acres of land form his father and thereafter died leaving defendant Nos. 36-51 as his heirs and successors. Abdul Aziz Bhuiyan got 9.134/9 acres of land from his father and died leaving defendant Nos. 53-63 as his heirs and successors. Ibrahim Bhuiyan got 9.04 acres of land from his father and he died leaving plaintiff Nos.1-4 and defendant Nos. 64 and 65 as his heirs and thus the plaintiffs got 6.03 acres of land out of the schedule I(Ka), I(Kha), I(Ga) and the 2nd schedule to the plaint.</u>

3. Further case of the plaintiff was that at the time of death of Alimuddin Bhuiyan his 2nd wife was pregnant and after his death his wife gave birth to a son namely, Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan- who subsequently died leaving defendant Nos. 66-76 as his heirs. That the heirs of CS recorded tenant Ashraf Ali, Anser Ali and Amjad Ali have been impleaded as defendant Nos. 77 to 81, That the defendant No. 1 Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan had transferred a portion of his property to different persons.

<u>4. The plaintiffs requested the defendants to make amicable partition, of their lands but the defendants denied and hence the suit. The plaintiffs claimed a separate saham for 6.04 acres of land.</u>

5. The defendant Nos. 66 to 76 the heirs of Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan contested the suit by filing written statements. The material case of these defendants was that by the deed of gift dated 29- 10-1911 Alimuddin Bhuiyan gifted 1/6 share of hisland to Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan, 1/6 share of Ibrahim Bhuiyan and 1/8 share to his 2nd wife and also gifted 1/8 share to each of his other 5 sons. Thereafter Foyter Nessa the 2nd wife of Alimuddin Bhuiyan died leaving behind 3 sons, namely, Md. Ibrahim Bhuiyan, Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan and Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan as her heirs. That since Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan was not born during the life time of his father Alimuddin Bhuiyan he did not get any property from his father by the deed of gift dated 29-10-1911.That in such circumstances his 2 full brothers Ibrahim Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan made an oral gift of 4.301/2 acres ofland out of their share to Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan and subsequently these 3 full brothers made a registered deed of partition on 16-5-1935 among themselves and according to that partition deed Ibrahim Bhuiyan got 6.671/2 acres of land, the defendant No.1 Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan got 4.33 acres of land and Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan got 4.301/2 acres of land. That Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan had purchased 0.46 decimal of land from the recorded owners Ashraf Ali and Ansar Ali by 2 separate registered deeds. Thus Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan got in all 4.761/2 acres of land and while he was in possession of his aforesaid land he died leaving behind defendant Nos. 66 to 76 as his heirs and successors. That the defendant No. 68, Rafiqul Islam purchased 0.09 acre of land from the recorded owner and thus the contesting defendant Nos. 66 to 76 got total 4.851/2 acres of land and they prayed for separate saham for that quantum of land.

6. The plaintiffs subsequently amended the plaint and stated that the alleged partition deed dated 15-6-1935 was false and forged, that Ibrahim Bhuiyan never gifted any land to Abdul Gafur and never executed and registered the alleged deed of partition. The plaintiffs,therefore prayed for declaration also that the alleged deed of partition dated 15-6-1935 was forged, fabricated, not acted upon and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

7. The trial court, on consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties and the facts and circumstances decreed the suit in part granting separate saham for 4.43 acres of land to the plaintiffs and also a separate saham for 4.851/2 acres of land to the contesting defendant Nos. 66 to 76. Against the said judgment and decree of the trial court the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 209 of 2007 before the learned District Judge, Comilla which was ultimately heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Comilla. This appellate Court, by the judgment and decree dated 1-1-2008, modified the judgment of the trial court and granted separate sahams for 4.42 acres of land to the plaintiffs and 4.53 and 1/2 acres of land to the defendant Nos. 66 to 67.

8. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the appellate court below the plaintiffs preferred Civil Revision No. 1394 of2008 and the contesting defendant Nos. 66 to 76 preferred Civil Revision No. 2821 of 2008 before the High Court Division. Rule was issued in both those civil revisions.

9. A Division Bench of the High Court Division heard both those Rules together and disposed of both those by a single judgment impugned in these two Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal. By this impugned judgment and order the High Court Division discharged the Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 1394 of 2008 and made the Rule absolute issued in Civil Revision No. 2821 of 2008 granting separate saham for 4.85 and 1/2 acres of land in favour of the contesting defendant Nos. 66 to 76.

10. Being aggrieved by this judgment and order of the High Court Division the plaintiff Nurul Hoq Bhuiyan alone has preferred both the present Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal.

11. We have heard Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner and Mr PC Guha, the learned Advocate for the contesting defendant-respondents.

12. Mr Mahmudul Islam has mainly argued to the effect that in this case the contesting defendants though have claimed that Ibrahim Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan gifted 4.30 and 1/2 acres of land to Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan their predecessor and subsequently executed and registered a deed of partition on 16-5-1935 allotting saham for 4.301/2 acres of land to Abdul Gafur, but this case of the contesting defendants have not been proved at all. The learned Counsel has argued also that though a certified copy of that alleged deed of partition dated 16-5-1935 has been filed before the court arid has been marked as exhibit-Kha, but it has not been properly taken into evidence; that the DW I who has produced this certified copy of the alleged partition deed dated 16-5-1935 had no personal knowledge about this alleged partition deed and she also did not state anything from whose custody this alleged deed of partition is coming, before the court.The learned Counsel has contended that for taking into evidence a certified copy of any registered deed the court is to be satisfied about the custody of this deed from where it is coming before the court and that since in this case the custody of this certified copy of the alleged partition deed has not been explained and proved the taking into evidence of this certified copy of the alleged partition deed and also marking of that as exhibit-Kha has been illegal and, as such, the decision taken by the courts below on the basis of this exhibit-Kha has been illegal and wrong. The learned Counsel for the plaintiff-leave-petitioner has argued also that the contesting defendants case that Ibrahim Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan gifted 4.30 and 1/2 acres of land to Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan also has not been proved by any evidence whatsoever and, in the circumstances the courts below committed wrong and illegality in allotting a share of that quantum of land to the contesting defendants.

13. Mr PC Guha has made submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division.

14. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate of both the side's and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and those of the appellate court below and the trial court.

15. It appears that all the 3 courts, on meticulous examination. and consideration of the evidence on record and the, other facts and circumstances, found that Ibrahim, Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan gifted 4.301/2,acres of land to their full brother Abdul, Gafur, Bhuiyan who was born after the death of their father, and as, such did not get any land from his father by the deed of gift dated 29-10-1911. It appears that all the courts below took into consideration the fact that Ibrahim Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan and their full brother Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan executed and registered a partition deed among themselves and in that partition deep they allotted a separate saham for 4.30 and 1/2 acres of land in  favour of Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan and opined that this registered partition deed-the Exhibit-Kha strongly supports the contesting defendants’ case that Ibrahim Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan orally gifted 4.30 and 1/2 acres of land to their younger brother Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan. The courts below took into consideration also that in all the records of right this land has duly been recorded in the name of Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan and after his death his heirs paid rent regularly for this land. The courts below pointed out also that Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan, the defendant No.1 and also other heirs of Ibrahim Bhuiyan the defendant Nos. 64 and 65 did not deny this oral gift by Ibrahim Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan in favour of Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan and also this partition deed of the year 1935 the exhibit-Kha and opined that this fact also strongly supported the defence case that Ibrahim Bhuiyan and Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan orally gifted 4.301/2acres of land in favour of Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan and subsequently they also executed and registered a partition deed the exhibit Kha allotting that quantum of land to Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan. The contention of the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-petitioner is that this partition deed dated 16-5-1935 the exhibit-Kha has not been proved and taken into evidence in accordance with law and, as such, the courts below committed illegality in putting reliance on this partition deed the exhibit-Kha. But we do not accept this contention of the learned Counsel for the leave-petitioner. This exhibit-Kha is an old registered deed of the year 1935 and, as such, is admissible in evidence without any formal proof. It appears that the DW1 who is the wife of the contesting defendant No.68 has produced this certified copy of the partition deed dated 16-5-1935 before the court and the court took this certified copy of the partition deed into evidence and has marked it as exhibit-Kha. Where there are ample facts and circumstance before the court as pointed out above in support of the genuineness of this partition deed and where this partition deed came before the court from the custody of the contesting defendants the heirs of one of the executants of this partition deed itself it cannot be said that this partition deed did not come before the court from the proper custody and, as such, taking of this partition deed into evidence and making of the same as exhibit has been illegal.

16. However, we find no merit in these two Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal. Rather, we find that the High Court Division, on meticulous examination and appreciation of the evidence on record and all other facts and circumstances, rightly held that the contesting defendant Nos.66 to 76 were entitled to get a separate saham for 4.851/2 acres of land and the plaintiffs are entitled to get a separate saham for 4.42 acres of land.

In the circumstances both these two Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal be dismissed.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 178 of 1966.
lawyer:
Moinul Huq with Meah Abdul Gafur ------ For the Appellant
T. Ali with Md Yahya ------ For the Respondent Nos. 1-8
parties:
Fakir Chand Mia being dead his heirs legal representatives Asadunnessa & ors  ------ Appellants.
Vs.
Qumaruzzaman & others  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya, J.- This appeal is at the instance of defendant No. 16 against a decree passed in a Suit for recovery of possession of 4 bighas of lands as described in the Schedule to the plaint on a declaration of the plaintiff's title thereto. Defendant Nos. 15 and 17 who were Respondent Nos. 23 and 24 in this appeal subsequently have got themselves transposed to the category of the appellants as Appellant Nos. 2 and 3.

2. Respondent Nos. 1 to 8 brought the suit in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca on the allegations 'inter alia' that the disputed lands appertaining to 5 C.S. plots, viz. plot Nos. 382,383, 384, 385 and 371 of Mouza Dhanmondi originally belonged to Jadav Chandra Singh and others who sold the same to Moulvi Mahatabuddin, the predecessor of the plaintiffs by a registered deed of sale, dated 22-9-1947 for a consideration of Rs.8000 that Moulvi Mahatabuddin having possessed the said land for some time on payment of rent to the landlord was dispossessed therefrom in the year 1952 by the defendants, that Moulvi Mahatabuddin died in March, 1959 leaving the plaintiffs as his heirs, that Defendant Nos. 1-14 were in actual possession of the disputed land alleging themselves to be tenants of defendant Nos. 15 to 19 and that the said defendants had no right, title and interest in respect of the said land.

3. The suit was contested by defendant Nos. 15-17 who filed a joint written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending 'inter alia' that the land of C. S. plot No. 384 appertaining to Khatian No. 222 and that of C. S. plot No. 383 appertaining to Khatian No. 180 along with the other lands belonged to Sree Nath Pashi and Jalim Pashi respectively, that after the death of Sreenath Pashi and abandonment of the holding by Jalim Pashi the landlord Tribeni Das Mohanta and Abdul Makim alias Ahsanullah took Khas possession of the same in 1933 that Defendant No.15 took settlement of 2 Bighas of land appertaining to C. S plot No. 384 from the landlord Tribeni Das Mohanra and constructed his home stead on a portion of the said land, that Tribeni Das Mohanta subsequently executed and registered a Patta in favour of Defendant No. 15 on the 11th February 1947, that in 1947 the said Defendant No. 15 took settlement of 46 acre of land apprising to C. S. plot No. 383 and 385 from Ahsanullah that Aktar Khatoon and others obtained a decree against Sreenat Pasni in Rent suit No. 638 of 1951 for arrear of rents in respect of Khatian No. 222 that in execution of the said decree, the holding recording in Khatian No. 222 was sold in auction which was subsequence set aside on the prayer of the Defendant No. 15 that a registered Patta was executed by Ahsanullah on the 27th December 1954 in favour of the said Defendant No. 15 in respect of the said Iand in confirmation of the previous that Defendant No 16 and his sister Fatu Bibi purchased 3 3/4 Kathas of land from Defendant No.15 out of the C.S. plot No. 383, that Defendant No. 17 purchased 2 Kathas of land on the 5th May, 1960 by a registered Kabala and that neither the plaintiffs nor their predecessor had ever possessed the disputed land, On the basis of the aforesaid pleadings the following issues were framed:-

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. is the suit bad for misjoinder and non joinder of parties?

3. Is the suit barred by adverse possession and limitation special and general.

4. Have the plaintiffs their alleged right, title and interest in the suit land.

5. Can the plaintiffs get a decree for declaration of their title and recovery of Khas possession on the grounds all age?

6. To what relief of any, were the plaintiffs entitled.

[Portion not necessary for reporting omitted]

4. As regard the first ground Mr. T. Ali, the learned advocate for the respondent frankly conceded and we think rightly that it was a case of non inclusion of a necessary party then the learned Subordinate Judge was clearly because in the absence of such persons the suit is not properly constituted and no effective decree can be passed by the Court. As to the second ground the proposition stated by learned Subordinate Judge is generally correct. Order 1, rule 13 or the Code of Civil Procedure provides as follows:-

"All objections on the ground of non-joinder or mis-joinder of married shall be taken at the earliest possible opportunity and in al cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement unless the ground of objection has subsequently arisen and any such ohiection not so taken shall be deemed to have been waived".

Any objection which does not enable the other side to take necessary steps to remove the defect is not to he taken any notice of. Mr. T. Ali, the learned Advocate for the respondent has relied upon the following observation made in the case of Jagadish Chandra Singha and another Vs Maharajdhiraj Dr. Sir Kameshwar Singh Babadur. A.I.R. 1953, Patna 178:

"It is essential that when an objection is raised to the frame of the suit on account of defect of parties,' it should be done at the earliest possible opportunity and the name of the persons omitted should be specifically mentioned so as to enable the other side to add those persons as parties to the suit if necessary. If this is not done the objection shall be deemed to have been waived".

Mr. T. Ali has submitted on the basis of this decision that since name of any other person apart from Fatu Bibi has not been mentioned in the written statement and possession of Fatu Bibi also has not been established, there is no substance in the contention of the appellant in this regard. Mr Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate for the respondent however relying upon the decisions in the case of Narain Panday and others Vs. Surajhan Lal & ors in AIR 1937 Pat 414 and in the case of Harun Sheikh & ors Vs Ramesh Chandra Bhattacharya and ors, 25 C.W.N. 249 has sought to argue that even if no such names have been mentioned in the written statement, but on the evidence adduced in the case it is found that some person whose presence is necessary for the effective determination of the dispute in the suit has not been impleaded in the suit and no effective decree can be passed in his absence, the Court is bound to take notice of the said fact The learned Advocate for the appellant has relied upon the following observation of Chief Justice Mukherjee, made in the case of Hasan Sheikh and ors Vs. Ramesh Chandra Bhattacharjee and ors as referred to above.

"Notwithstanding the provisions of Or. 1. r. 1.9 of the Civil Procedure Code, the Court will not entertain a suit in which no effective decree can be made in the of an interested party, If it is discovered that a person interested in the servant tenement bas not been made a party to the suit, the Court will not proceed to make a decree. The decree if made must be infructuous; if a suit is instituted by the absent person for an injunction to restrain the plaintiff from executing the decree there is not possible answer to the prayer".

We respectfully agree with the view taken the said case of Calcutta High Court. It is one of the established principles of judicial procedure that [no Court should pass a decree which is infructuous any can he set at naught at the will of a person who has not been made a party to the suit.]

5. On the evidence adduced in the case we do not think that the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in taking the view that there is no satisfactory evidence about possession of any non-empleaded parties. The contesting defendants have adduced some evidence to show that Fatu Bibi and one Ismail who are not parties to the suit are in possession of some portion of the disputed land. As regards Ismail, nothing has been mentioned in the written statement. In the evidence given by D W.4 who is an unsummoned witness, there is a statement to the effect that to the east of Rahim Bux's house and to the south of Abdul Razzak's house is the house of Ismail Shabed. It has not been definitely stated that Ismail's house stands on a portion of the disputed land D.W 5 alone says that Ismail's house is upon the disputed land. In view of the absence of any pleading in this respect, it difficult to hold reliving upon this piece of evidence that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in his assessment that Ismail was not a necessary the suit. But the Question of Fatu Bibi stands on a different footing. It has been clearly asserted in the written statement that Fakir Chand and his sister Fatu Bibi purchased a portion of C.S 383 from Defendant No. 15 on 30-11-54 and have built a residential house where they have been living with their families. The registered deed of sale by which Rahim Bux sold the said land to Fakir Chand and Fatu Bibi has been marked Ext B(1). Fakir Chand has been made Defendant in the suit on the allegation that Defendant Nos. 1-14 are in actual occupation alleging that they are tenants under Defendant Nos. 15-17. The case sought to be made out at the trial was that the Defendant was in possession but they were trespassers. So, we think it cannot be successfully assailed that Fakir Chand who claims on the basis of Ext. B(1) is in possession of a portion of the disputed land, as included in Ext B(1). In that view of the matter the possession of Fatu Bibi can hardly be disputed. In our view [Fatu Bibi was a necessary party to the suit but due to her absence, the entire suit can not fail. The plaintiffs can be non-suited only in respect of the land appertaining to C. S. plot No. 383 because it is only in this plot in which Fatu Bibi is interested and is in possession.]

6. Mr. Tofazzal Ali the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents has contended that the statement made in para 2 of Ext. 1 cannot be used in evidence as the attention of P W. 3 the maker of the said statement, was not drawn to it while he was giving his testimony in the witness box. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has cited a Full Bench decision of Lahore High Court in the case of Firm Malik Des Raj Faquir Chand Vs Firm Pyyara Lal Aya Ram and ors AIR. 1946 Lahore 65. It has been held in the said decision that if the maker of a previous statement has been examined as a witness in a case and has made a statement in his testimony which is contrary to his previous statement and his attention has not been drawn to the contradicrion occuring in his previous statement the said statement cannot be used in evidence in view of the provision of section 145 of the Evidence Act.

7. It appears a conflict of judicial views arose in the decisions of Indian High Courts centering round the interpretation of the provisions of section 21 and section 145 of the Evidence Act and two decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Counci, Viz Chandra Kumar Vs. Chowdhury Narpat Singh, LR. 34 Ind, App 27 same case ILR 29 All 184 and Bal Gangadhar Tilak Vs. Shri Niwas Pandit LR 42 Ind Appeal 135 same case AIR 1915 P.C. have been cited as authorised for the respective views on the question of the applicability of the provision of section 145 of the Evidence Act to an admisson contained in a previous statement of a party who has made a statement in his testimony inconsistent with his previous admission.

8. In the case of Chandra Kumar Vs. Chaudhury Narpat Singh (34 Ind App.27) the plaintiff Mukund Singh came to the Court with the allegation that he was the son of Partap Singh whose natural son admittedly he was and as such was entitled to the estate through him. The defendant sought to defeat the claim of plaintiff by producing two deeds-one a deed of gift and another a power of attorney-both executed by Mukund Singh. But these contained clear admissions by the plaintiff showing that he was the adopted son of Kishan Singh, elder brother of Partap Singh, Mukund Singh while deposing as a witness set up a case inconsistent with his admission in the said deeds but he was not confronted with those  admissions while in the witness box. Despite this, these admissions were considered to be fully admissible by their Lordships of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council who went on to make the following significant pronouncement after observing that the burden of proving the adoption lay undoubtedly with the defendant:

"But it is difficult to conceive how she could as against Mukund Singh prima Janie at all events discharge that burden more effectually than by proving his solemn statement under hand and seal that it did take place. The proof of this admission shifts the burden.”

 The case of Bal Gangadhar Tilak Vs. Shri Niwas Pandit (42 Ind. Appeal 135) was also a case of a disputed adoption in which the plaintiff Jagannath sought to establish that he was the validly adopted son of one Shri Baba Maharaj. Bal Gangadhar Tilak being one of the Trustees impleaded himself as one of the plaintiffs. Certain minutes and letters written by Mr. Tilak in which he recorded a detailed account of the proceedings of adoption were produced in this case. Their Lordships of the Privy Council relied on the oral evidence of Mr. Tilak as well as those documents and letters and upheld the plaintiff's claim on the view that all these documents taken together complete, confirmed his case in the witness box and that there was no ground in fact for the conclusions that they either contradicted the testimony or cast any reasonable doubt upon it. Their Lordships, however strongly disapproved of the use made by the learned Judges of the High Court of certain ambiguous expressions contained in the documents written by Mr. Tilak in giving an inferential verdict of perjury against Mr. Tilak and in disbelieving his evidence and made the following observation in this regard:

"But the must also record their dissent from the view that the case made of these documents in this case was justified by law. On general principles it could appear to be sound that if a witness is under cross-examination on oath he should be given the opportunity if the documents are to be used against him, to tender his explanation and to clear up the particular point of ambiguity or dispute. This is a general salutory and intelligible rule and where witness's reputation and character are at stake the duty of enforcing this rule could appear to be sigillary clear.” 

Then after quoting section 145, Evidence Act, their Lordships further observed:

"Had the safeguards set up by the law with respect to the use of documents been observed? Not at all. Not only have documents been used for the purpose of contradicting witnesses without obeying the injunctions prescribed by law, but the inference thus derived, and improperly derived from the documents has resulted as stated in an inferentual verdict of perjury."

 It should be noticed that no reference has been made in this case to sec 21 of the Evidence Act nor any dissent has been expressed as to pronouncement of law made in Chandra Kumar's case (34 Ind. App 27) on the question of a previous admission shifting the burden of proof.

9. The earliest case in the Indian subcontinent after the Privy Council decision in Bal Gangadhar Tilak's case appears to be a case of the Calcutta High Court in Upendra Nath Vs. Bhupendra Nath reported in 21 C.W.N-280 same case A.I.R. 1916 Cal 110 which without referring to Chandra Kumar's case but relying upon Bal Gangadhar Tilak's case heId that certain statements of the parties which were inconsistent with the evidence given by them in Court could not be used in evidence as they were not put to them.

 10. The next case Shafiquddin Vs. Mahboob Elahi is of Lahore High Court reported in AI R. 1930 Lah 715 in which it was held that a previous statement containing an admission of a, party was not admissible unless it was put to the party. Similar view was taken in the case of Latafat Hossain Vs. Onkar Mal reported in AIR- 1935 Oud 41. A Division Bench of Patna High Court however took a contrary view in Ramkeshwar Vs. Daldes Singh reported, in A I.R 1936 Pat. 588 which held that an admission of a party which had been proved in the case was substantive evidence under sec 21 Evidence Act and its admissibility was not affected by the question whether it was put to the party or not. Its view was pressed after referring to Bal Gangadhar Tilak's case in the following manner:

"It is an admission which goes to the root of the case, which is relevant under sec. 21 Evidence Act; and its relevancy is not affected by the question of whether the defendant may or may not have given evidence consistent with the statement contained and if it had been a document which had no relevancy apart from the fact that it contained contradicted statements made by the defendant when he was in the witness box it could have been necessary to observe strictly the provisions of sec. 145……”  

11. Because of the conflicting judicial views as have been just referred to there was a reference to a full Bench of the Lahore High Court in the case of Firm Malik Desarj Faquir Cfand Vs. Firn Pyyaralal Aya Lal reported 1946 Lah. 65 (F.B.) which has been mentioned above and the Full Bench affirmed the view taken in the case reported in A.I.R. 1930 Lah. 714 and dissented from the view taken by the Patna High Court in A.I.R. 1936 Pat. 588. The statement of law as has been pronounced in the said Full Bench case and relied on in the present case by Mr. Tofazzal Ali, the learned Advocate for the respondent has been based upon an interpretation of the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council given in Bal Gangadhar Tilak's case.

12. It should be noticed however that the Privy Council decision in Chandra Kumar's case (34 Ind. App. 27) in which a previous admission of the plaintiff of the suit contained in two deeds was accepted as good evidence, although the same was not put to him, when he was examined as a witness was not considered or referred to in the said decision of the Full Bench of the Lahore High Court, since the aforesaid Full Bench decision of Lahore High Court, some of the High Courts of Indian jurisdiction including the High Court of Calcutta followed the Lahore view, but the High Court of Allahabad, in the case of Must. Ulfat Vs. Zubaida Khatoon reported in A I.R. 1955 All. 361, after referring to both of the Privy Council decisions, viz. Chandra Kumar's case (34 Ind. App. 27) and Bal Gangadhar Tilak's case (42 Ind. App. 135) dissented from the view of the Lahore Full Bench in A.I.R. 1946 Lah. 65 and held that sec. 145. Evidence Act did not apply when the witness was a party whose admission had already been proved under sec.21 of the Act. When shortly after the same question came before another Bench of Allahabad High Court, there was a reference to a Full Bench namely Ajadhya Parsad Vs. Bhawani Shankar reported in A.I.R. 1957 All 1 (F.B.), which by a majority has held that where in a civil suit a party produce documents containing clear and unambiguous admission the party producing these documents can be permitted under sec.21 Evidence Act to use them as substantive evidence in the case without drawing in cross-examination the attention of the opponent to those admissions. It however the admissions are ambiguous or vague it has been further held, it is obligatory on the party who relies on them to draw in cross, examination the attention of the opponent to the said statements before he can be permitted to use them for the purpose of contradicting the evidence on oath of the opponent.

13. It has been pointed out in the said case that the Judicial Committee did not express any dissent in the later case of Bal Gangadhar Tilak (42 Ind. App. 135) from the statement of law as to the admissibility of a document containing an admission of a party as made in the earlier case of Chandra Kumar (34 Ind. App. 27) and that the Judicial Committee in Bal Gangadhar Tilak's case deprecated the use of certain expressions of doubtful import occurring in some earlier documents which according to the Judicial Committee, were wholly consistent with the oral testimony of the writer of those document solely for the purpose of contradicting him without giving him an opportunity to explain those ambiguous and doubtful expressions. According to the Judicial Committee, the provision of sec. 145 Evidence Act has its application only in such a case. The Supreme Court of India in an appeal from a decision of the Punjab (India) High Court which did not permit the use of certain admission, of the defendant contained in some documents as the defendant when in the witness box was not confronted with these admissions had to consider this question and give their opinion in the said case of Bharat Singh and others Vs. Mst. Bhagirathi reported in 1966 (S C) 405 dissenting from the opinion of the Lahore Full Bench and approving of that of the Allababad Full Bench in the following manner :—

"The legal objection to the consideration of these admissions was based on the Full Bench decision of the Punjab High Court in Firm Malik Des Raj Vs. Firm Piara Lal A I.R. 1946 Lah. 65 (F B.). The view taken in that case was differed to by the Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court in Ajodhya Prasad Vs. Bhawami Shankar A.IR. 1957 All. 1 (F.B). The Punjab High Court based its decision on the observations of the Privy Council in Bal Gangadhar Tilak Vs. Shrinivas Pandit (42 Ind. App.135) (A.I R. 1915 P.C. 7). That case, however, did not directly deal with the use of admissions which are proved but are not put to the person making the admissions when he enters the witness box. The entire tenor of the documents whose certain contents were construed by the High Court to discredit the persons making those admissions went to support their case and did not in any way support the case of the other party. File Privy Council expressed its disapproval of the High Court minutely examining the contents of the documents and using its own inferences from those statements to discredit the oral statements of the persons responsible for making those documents when those per sons had not been confronted with those statements in accordance with s. 145 of the Indian Evidence Act. Admissions have to be clear if they are to be used against the person making them.

Admissions are substantive evidence by themselves in view of ss. 17 and 21 of the Indian Evidence Act though they are not conclusive proof of the matters admitted. We are of opinion that the admissions duly proved are admissible evidence irrespective of whether the party making them appeared in the witness box or not and whether that party when appearing as witness was confronted with those statements in case he made a statement contrary to those admissions. The purpose of contradicting the witness under s. 145 of the Evidence Act is very much different from the purpose of proving the admission. Admission is substantive evidence of the fact admitted while a previous statement used to contradict a witness does not become substantive evidence and merely serves the purpose of throwing doubt on the veracity of the witness. What weight is to be attached to an admission made by a party is a matter different from its use as admissible evidence.''

In Pakistan a Division Bench of the Lahore High Court in the case of Ghulam Nabi Corporation Vs. Iftikhar Hussain Khan reported in P L.D. 1962 Lahore 370 held without referring to any case-law whatsoever, that a statement which was intended to be used as an admission of a party could be used against him even though the formalities laid down in sec. 145 of the Evidence Act were not complied with, as it was relevant under sec. 21 of tile Evidence Act. In a case before a Division Bench of Dacca High Court constituted by Amiruddin Ahmed C. J. and Rahman J (Muhammad Mustafa Chowdhury Vs. Sudhanshu Bimal Biswas and another reported in 8 DLR (38) the principle laid down in the Full Bench case of Lahore High Court (A.I.R 1946 Lah. 65) was sought to be applied to an oral admission and Rahman, J. as he then wasp pointed out that the answer given by the Full Bench extended the principle of sec. 145 of the Evidence Act to the case of admission by parries reduced into writing but did not apply to oral admissions. The correctness of the Lahore decision does not appear to have been disputed before that Bench. A single Bench of the Dacca High Court (Murshed C. J.) in the case of Ananta Kumar Vs. Sebarate Ulba reported in 17 DLR (Dacca) 626 same ease P.L.D. 1966 Dacca 114 followed the Lahore Full Bench decision and set aside a judgment on the ground of treating an admission of a party contained in a written statement filed by him in an earlier suit as evidence in the case without complying with the requirements of sec. 145 Evidence Act.

14. Subsequently this question came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Malik Din vs. Mohammad Aslam reported in 21 D.L.R. (S C) 94. In that case a question was raised as to whether a Collector's which contained an admission of the plaintiff on a material point involved in the suit could be used as evidence without complying with the requirements of Sec. 145, Evidence Act. Hamoodur Rahman, J (as he then was) delivering the judgment of the Bench observed as follows :—

"The next contention of the learned Counsel is that in any event the recital could not be used against Malik Din, without confronting him with it as required by section 145 of the Evidence Act. This argument is again misconceived; as such confrontation is necessary only for the purpose of contradiction. In the present however the purpose for which the recital was sought to be utilised was to induce the Court to draw the inference that the present case sought to he made out through the plaintiff Imam Din was an afterthought for on the previous occasion, no such case was made out. No confrontation was therefore necessary".

Although in this case no case-law has been discussed nor elaborate Nast ns have been given in support of the decision taken the view of the Court was clearly expressed. The formalities required under sec. 145 of the Evidence Act need not be observed in a case where a previous statement is sought to be used for any purpose other than mere contradiction of the witness provided the same is admissible in evidence under some other provision of the Evidence Act.

15. We find ourselves in respectful agreement with the view expressed by the Supreme Court of India and the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the cases referred to above and this view of the law is well supported by the pronouncement of the judicial Committee in the case of Chandra Kumar Vs Chaudhri Narpat Singh 34 IA. 74. Tile reasonableness of this view will be apparent from a careful consideration of the language used in section 145 of the Evidence Act which is to the following effect:

''A witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing or reduced into writing and relevant to Matters in question without such writing being shown to him or being proved but if it is intended to contradict him by the writing his attention must before the writing can be proved be recalled to those parts of it which are to be used for the purpose of contradicting him."

From the language used in the said provision it is clear that the previous statement, reference to which has been made in the said section has not yet been proved but which is sought to be proved for the purpose of contradiction a particular witness deposing in the witness box. This provision cannot, in our opinion, be interpreted to be referring to a statement which has already been proved as substantive evidence in the said very proceeding under some other provision of the Evidence Act. We think it cannot be argued with any reasonableness that a statement which has already been proved either as an admission under section 21 of the Evidence Act or under some other provision of the Act and has become a part of the records it shall cease to be evidence in the case and go out of the record if the maker of the statement examined as a witness chooses to make a statement contrary to his previous statement and his attention is not drawn to it. It can certainly be said that it if the only relevancy of such a statement is in its use for the purpose of contradicting a witness and opportunity has not been given to him to explain the said contradiction it should not be used for the purpose of contradicting him but if it is substantive evidence under some other provision of the Evidence Act it does not appear to be in consonance with good reason that it should cease to be evidence not-withstanding clear provision of the Evidence Act in respect of admissibility of evidence.

16. We are, therefore unable to accept the contention of Mr. T. Ali that the statement in Ext. 1 cannot he used in evidence because Mvi. Ahsanullah the maker of the statement was not confronted in the witness box with the statement made in Ext. 1. The said exhibit is admissible as substantive evidence as an admission under section 21 Evidence Act against Ahsanullah P. W. 3 as the maker of the statement as well as against the plaintiffs being the representatives in interest of the said maker and also as a transaction for instance under sec. 13 of the Evidence Act.

17. Before we part with this appeal, we are to dispose of 3 applications which have been filed in this appeal on behalf of the appellants. Two of the applications are for accepting certain documents as additional Evidence. Under Order 41 rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the other is for adding under President's Order No. 142 of 1972 the Government of Bangladesh as party in this appeal.

18. So far as the question of additional evidence is concerned, the documents which are sought to he proved in this case relate to a certain transactions effacing transfer of certain portion of the disputed land at various points of time. These documents may be evidence relating to possession of various persons at certain points of lime in the past but we do not think that these are of such a nature as this Court requires them of the purpose of dispose of the appeal. We therefore, reject these applications for additional evidence.

19. The other is for adding the Government of Bangladesh as a party in view of the provision of President’s Order No. 142 of 1972. It is stated in this application that if it is held that the Government is a necessary party in that case the Government may be added as a party in this appeal before its disposal. We do not think it is the legislative intent of the said Presidential Order that the Government should be made a party in such a case.

20. The preamble of President’s Order No. 142 of 1972 which has been called the Bangladesh Transfer of Immoveable Property (temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 runs thus:

"Whereas it is expedient to make provisions retracting the transfer of immovable property in Bangladesh h in public interest.” The Article 6 of the said Order is to the following effect No person shall without joining the Government which shall he a necessary party, file of proceed with any Suit.

(a) For the specific performance of any contract relating to the transfer of any immovable property or for declaration of title to or assertion of ownership of any such property.

(b) for enforcement of mortgage security in relation to any immovable property except where the mortgage is the movement or a local authority or a scheduled Bank or a statutory Corporation or a cooperative Society or

(c) for partition of immovable property where total area of the property involved exceeds one hundred standard “bighas.”

Now, the question is whether suit fur declaration of title or assertion of ownership as is contemplated in clause (a) of the said Article is the kind of suit out of which the present appeal arises. The obvious object of the legislation as found in the preamble of the Order and also in its substantive provisions appears to be the prevention of certain transfers of immovable property in derogation of some legislative enactments. If we keep this document purpose of the enactment in view, it will be clear that the words "any such property" as used in clause (a) or the Article will not be preferable to any immovable property, but to any immovable property which was the subject matter of a tract relating to transfer. To interpret this provision in any other way so as to make it applicable to any suit for declaration of title to or assertion of ownership of any immovable property does not appear to be reasonable at all because that will make this provision absolutely pointless and needlessly harassing. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the provision of Article 6 of the President's Order No.142 of 1972 bas no application to the present case and so the Government of Bangladesh is not a necessary party in this case.

21. The result is that this appeal is allowed, judgment any decree of the Court below set aside and the suit is dismissed. Having regard to the fact and circumstances of the case there shall be no order as to costs and we direct that is parties shall hear their own costs throughout.

Fazle Munim. J, I agree.

End.
