full_judgment:
This Rule on an application under Section 115(1) of the Cede of Civil Procedure (in short, the CPC) filed by the defendant-petitioners was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-12 to show cause as to why Judgment and decree dated 22-2-2004 passed by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Bogra in Other Class Appeal No. 28 of 2004 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 11-11-2001 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Shariakandi , bogra in Eviction Suit No, 57 of 1 997 dismissing the suit, should not be set-aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that the present opposite-party Nos. 1-12 as plaintiffs instituted above numbered suit for the eviction of the present defendant-petitioners and opposite Party Nos. 13-16 from the suit land appertaining to CS plot No, 364 and 368 of CS khatian 46 of Tajruparamouja under Shariakandi Police Station of Bogra district comprising an area of 1,77 acres of land averring inter-alia that the land of CS khatian No, 46 was correctly recorded In the name of Meherullah Akond, Esharat Akond, Topljan Bibi, Serna Bibi, Syednesa Bibi, Panes Uddin Mondal, Idris Mondan, Ajirunnessa, Nojlbunnesa and Asmat ullah Mendalln different share.

3. One of the recorded tenant Meherullah Akond died leaving wife Kosiran Bibi and daughter Halima Khatun, While Kesiranbibi was possessing 1.77 acres of land and which is suit land also sold by a registered kabala on 13-11-1936 to Keramatullah Mia, Fazlar Rahman" the predecessor of the plaintiffs and Ator All Mia, the predecessor of the defendant-petitioners, Halima khatun died leaving daughter Waheda Khatun who sold 5.00 acres of land by a registered kabala on 11-5-1946 to the plaintiff No.4 of the suit. Fazlar Rahman died leaving the plaintiffs thus the plaintiffs have been possessing the land inherited by them from their predecessor Fazlor Rahman erecting dwelling huts and cultivating the rest land therein.

4. One of the recorded tenant Esharat Ali died leaving daughter Fatema Khatun who filed Partition Suit No. 150 of 1951 for the partition of the land of CS khatian No. 46. In the said suit, Fazlar Rahman, the predecessor of the plaintiffs was defendant No. 16, the present plaintiff No.4 was defendant No. 23 and Ator Ali, the predecessor of the defendants was defendant No. 10. ln the said Partition Suit some of the defendants filed written statements in order to contest the suit and some of the co-sharers prayed for saham.

5. The said suit was decreed finally on 14-1- 1957 and pursuant to the said decree the suit land along with other lands were allotted in the saham of Fazlar Rahman and the plaintiff Nos. 1/3-4 but no share of land was allotted in favour of Ator Ali, the predecessor of the defendants thus he became land less in the suit holding and under the said prevailing circumstances he had requested his elder brother Fazlar Rahman to continue into the suit land.

6. Since Fazlar Rahman used to serve in the police department he did not usually reside in his native dwelling hut on the suit land and in the vacation he and his family members used to visit the dwelling hut casually from time to time and under above facts and circumstance Fazlar Rahman allowed his younger brother Ator Ali to live on the suit land during his life time. Fazlar Rahman also asked his sons and daughter not to disturb Ator Ali to live on the suit land during his life time and accordingly though the defendants were trying to grab the suit land in this or that way but heirs of Fazlar Rahman did not disturb Ator Ali for the "asiyat" of their predecessor Fazlar Rahman.

7. Ator Ali died on 29-5-1997 leaving the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and Nasiruddin as sons and defendant No.5 as wife. The plaintiffs requested the defendants to surrender the vacant possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs on 16-7-1997 and though they assured the plaintiffs that within 15 days there of they will vacate the suit land but ultimately they did not leave the suit land and accordingly the plaintiffs again requested the defendants on 16-8-1997 to hand over the vacant possession of the suit land in their favour but the defendants denied the same. Hence the plaintiffs have been constrained to file the suit.

8. The defendant Nos. 2, 6 and 7 filing a joint written statement denied the material allegations of the plaint. The case of the defendants, in short, is that 71.92 acres of land appertaining CS to khatian No. 46 originally belong to Meherullah Akond and others in different share who mortgaged the land to Naimullah Fakir and accordingly CS khatian No. 76 was prepared in the name of Naimullah Fakir. One Kobej Mollah was the borgader under the Naimullah Fakir as such CS khatian No. 77 was also prepared in the name of Kobej Mollah articulating his possession thereon.

9. For the arrear of rents, the entire land of Tajruparamouja along with the lands of 9 other, moujas were sold in an auction and since there was no purchaser, the Deputy Commissioner Bogra, purchased the said land in the auction. The Deputy Commissioner was inducted into the possession of the said land and the tenancy of the former tenants were annuled through the case No. 126(12)53-54.

10. The Deputy Commissioner took initiative for the settlement of said land among the people of that locality and one Amzadur Rahman took settlement of 2.99 acres of land from the Deputy Commissioner Bogra, on 5-2-1956 through the settlement case No. 196(12) 66-67. Amzadur Rahman set Ator Ali, the predecessor of the defendants to look after the said land and Ator Ali with the permission of Amzadur Rahman erected house on the land of plot No. 364. Amzadur Rahman sold .37 acres of land on 26-10-1988 to defendant No.1. The defendants entered into an agreement on 15-3-1997 with Amzadur Rahman to purchase 1.77 acres of land from him Amzadur Rahman also sold some land on different date to the defendants, thus the defendants have been possessing the suit land acquiring the same from Amzadur Rahman. The plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession into the suit land the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost.

11. Upon the above pleadings, the trial Court framed as many as 6 issues to dispose of the suit whereupon the plaintiffs examined 6 witnesses and filed some documentary evidences which has been marked as exhibits- 1 to 6 and the contesting defendants examined 4 witnesses and filed some documentary evidences which has been marked as exhibit K- Tha and the trial Court considering the evidence and other materials on record dismissed the suit by his judgment dated 11-11-2001. Against the said judgment, the plaintiffs preferred title appeal No. 28 of 2002 in the Court of District Judge Bogra which has been heard by the Additional district Judge 3rd Court, Bogra who by his impugned judgment dated 22-2-2004 reversing the judgment of the trial Court, decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. The defendant-petitioners being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with said judgment and decree of the appellate Court below dated 22-2-2004 moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

12. Mr Md Abdul Jabbar along with Md Ibrahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners supports the Rule. He submits that the plaintiffs filed the suit for eviction of the defendants from the suit land but the plaintiffs could not show and manifest in the plaint as to from when the defendants or their predecessor Ator Ali was possessing the suit land under them as permissive possessor. He categorically submits that in fact the defendants had been possessing the suit land from 13-11-1936 when their predecessor Ator Ali and Fazlar Rahman, the predecessor of the plaintiffs had purchased 1.77 acres of land from Kosirannesa, the wife of recorded tenant Meherullah Akond. He also submits that a partition suit being No. 150 of 1951 was filed where the Ator Ali, the predecessor of defendants was defendant No.1 0 and from the materials on record it appears that the defendant No. 10 in that suit neither filed a written statement nor prayed for saham but for that reasons his share and right title in the suit land will not be extinguished in any way. There is no paper to show that Ator Ali was even evicted in pursuant of the final decree of that partition suit. He also submits that possession of the defendants is admitted in the suit and in fact Ator Ali and his heirs have been possessing the suit land from 1936 as their purchased land, so the eviction of such original owner from their own land is neither possible nor desirable.

13. He further submits that the trial Court categorically found that the plaintiffs could not prove the title and possession into the suit land but the appellate Court below without giving any reasons whatsoever found the title of the plaintiffs into the suit land and this sort of findings of the appellate Court below is against the provisions of law. He submits that Order XLI Rule 31 CPC provides that the appellate Court must record reasons of its decision but the appellate Court below without assigning the reasons reversed the judgment of the trial Court and thereby committed an error of law resulted into an error into the decision occasioning failure of justice to the defendant-petitioners and, as such, the judgment and order of the appellate Court below is liable to be set-aside making the Rule absolute.

14. Mr Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties opposes the Rule. He submits that the trial Court on the wrong assessment of the evidence on found that the plaintiffs have no title into the suit land but the appellate Court below on due consideration of the evidence and other materials on record came to a right conclusion that the plaintiffs had acquired title into the suit land and after the final decree of former partition suit No. 150 of 1951, Ator Ali, the predecessor of the defendants became landless and the appellate Court below also rightly found that the defendants could not prove his case adducing any cogent and nitid oral and documentary evidences thus the appellate Court below did not commit any error of law and fact in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties as such the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

15. At the fanged of the hearing of this Rule, the learned. Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties submitting a petition sought amendment in the plaint of the original suit. In the said petition it was articulated that after the final decree of the partition suit on 16-3-1957, Ator Ali' sought permission to stay in the suit land and his full brother Fazlar Rahman allowed him to continue with his possession into the suit land on and from 17- 3-1957 as his permissive possessor. The learned Advocate for the opposite-parties also submits that for removing any kind of confusion in the suit, the amendment sought today would be helpful.

16. I have considered the above submissions of the learned Advocates of both the parties with profound attention and have gone through the materials on record.

17. On going to the materials on record it appears that the plaintiffs filed the suit for eviction of the defendants from the suit land claiming them (defendants) as their permissive possessor but the plaint was totally silent as to from when the defendants were inducted into the suit land as their permissive possessor and infact to address this lacuna of the plaint, the plaintiff-opposite parties sought the amendment today as stated herein- before.

18. The learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners in this regards submits that the total case of the plaintiffs is centered around this point that as to from when they (defendants) were allegedly inducted into the possession of the suit land as their permissive possessor and since the plaint is totally silent on this vital point, the trial Court rightly held there was no cause of action of the present suit and the plaintiffs at this stage to fill up the lacuna sought the amendment which they cannot do at all and if the amendment as sought for is allowed that will be simple in justice to the defendant-petitioners and an undue premium to the plaintiffs. He also submits that the date as has been shown in the amendment is a question of fact which cannot be answered through the momentary hearing of the Rule rather the defendant-petitioners require to submit additional 'writ": ten statements but if the same is done at this stage that will be cumbersome for all.

19. From the plaint and other materials on record it appears that by the deed of 13-11-1936 Fazlar Rahman and Ator Ali and their father had acquired 1.77 acres of land which is the suit land now, from Kosirannesa, the wife of recorded-tenant Meherullah Akond. So, we find that Ator Ali, the predecessor of the defendants had every reason to be in possession of the suit land at his own accord and it is also fact that during the partition suit being No. 150 of 1951 though the Ator Ali was the defendant No. 10, but he neither filed written statements nor prayed for saham. But if anybody who had acquired land in a partiable land, do not pray for saham in a partition suit his right, title and interest will not be extinguished in anyway.

20. Moreso, from the commissioner report of that partition suit, exhibit 1(a) goes to show that-in page No.4, the advocate commissioner at the time of allotment of the land in the field noticed the ownership of Ator Ali along with the Fazlar Rahman and Keramotullah into the partible through the kabala dated 13-11-1936. But it is very astonishing' and surprising to me that the defendant in their written statements denied this kabala . although, the learned advocate for the defendant-petitioners submits that in fact the defendant being misconceived and misconstrued of the fact-denied the said kabala erroneously and which was a blatant error on the part of the defendants and also on the part of their lawyer who had conducted, the, suit on their behalf at trail. However, I feel that there should no comment on this submission of the learned advocate for the petitioners at this stage of the proceeding.

<u>21. The defendants in their very disheveled and wishy-washy written statements adverted many thing's but proved nothing at trial. The written statement occupies some important facts that the entire land of Tajru pant mouja along with the lands 9 other moujas were sold in an auction arising out of the rent suits, but the written statement did not disclose the names of the parties and the numbers of the rent suit. It was further adverted in the written statement that through the case No. 126(l2) 53-54 the tenancy of the former tenants were annulled but there, appears no documents in support of this important contention, Though the defendants filed papers marked exhibit 'Ga' to show that Amzadur Rahman took settlement of 2.99 acres of land from the government through settlement case No. 196(12) 6667 but this, document did not contain the particulars of the suit land. So it is difficult for, this court to come into a fair conclusion that-by exhibit, 'Ga' Amzadur Rahman, the predecessor in interest of the defendants took settlement of the suit land from the government.</u>

22. The defendants could have claimed the suit land as their own relying on the kabala dated 13-11-1936 very easily .and sharply but it.is not under stood as to, why the defendants had disowned the Same. However, be that as it may, now, come to the fact of seeking amendment to day again.

23. In a suit for' eviction of the defendants from a particular land it is always important for the plaintiffs to disclose as to from when the defendants were inducted into possession in to the suit land but the plaint was more or less, silent till today from the date of filing on 27-8-1997. Since the learned advocate for the defendant-petitioners finds that the defendants were inducted into the possession into the suit land on the basis of kabala dated 13-11-1936. So, I find that if the suit is sent back on remand for trial afresh giving a chance to the plaintiffs and the defendants to amend their pleadings and to adduce further evidence on the said amendments that will be a proper course to render the justice to both the parties. It is also pertinent to point out that amendment of the pleadings is always justified if the same is found to be necessary for the purpose of determining the real question of controversy between the parties. Since in the present suit, the real controversy between parties appears to be as to from when the defendants wert inducted into possession of the suit land is the subject matter of the amendment, so if the suit is remanded back that will serve the purpose of the ends of justice. Since I have taken the decision to sent the suit back on remand upon set- ting aside the impugned judgment and decree of the appellate Court below it will be beneficial for both parties not to be more details on any other point.

24. Having regards to the above discussion, the original-suit is sent back on remand to the trial Court upon setting-aside the impugned judgment of the appellate Court below.

25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the original suit is sent back on remand to the trial Court for trial afresh. The trial Court will allow both the plaintiffs and defendants to amend their plaint and written statement and to adduce further evidence in support of their amended pleadings and thereafter pronounce the judgment afresh.

Let a copy of this judgment and order along with the lower. Courts record be sent down to the concerned .Court for, information and necessary action.

End.

parties:
Birendra Chandra Saha  ------- Appellant 
Vs. 
Sashi Mohan Saha and others  ------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 29-6-1966 passed by the Dacca High Court in F.A No. 91 of 1961).
full_judgment:
Muhammad Abdullah Jabir, J.—This appeal by special leave arises out of a judgment of the erstwhile High Court of East Pakistan in an appeal arising out of a suit which was filed by the plaintiff-appellant for declaration of his title to the disputed land and buildings and structure standing thereon and for recovery of possession of the same and for mesne profits. The suit was decreed by the learned Subordinate Judge; Dacca who tried the same but, on appeal by the defendant-respondents, the learned Judges of the High Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit. Thereafter the plaintiff filed a petition for special leave to appeal in the erstwhile Supreme Court of Pakistan which granted the leave prayed for.

2. The plaintiff instituted the suit claiming to have taken a permanent lease of the suit property by registered deed from one Modhusudan Saha for a consideration of Rs. 12,000/- on the 22nd November, 1951. The plaintiff was liable to pay rent to Modhusudan Shaha on account of the lease at the rate of 4 annas per annum and, by another deed of sale executed on the same date. Modhusudan Saha sold his right to receive the aforesaid rent to the plaintiff for a sum of Rs. 40/- only and thus the plaintiff acquired 16 annas interest in the suit property. According to the further case of the plaintiff the defendant No. 1 Sashi Mohan Saha and his brother late Lai Mohan Saha who were occupying a part of the buildings as tenants under Modhusudan Saha at a rental of Rs. 125/- per annum, took the entire buildings from the plaintiff on rent at a rental of Rs. 50/- per month. The defendant No.1 paid a sum of Rs. 50/- as rent for one month in advance to the plaintiff in Ashar, 1359 B.S. and thereafter did not pay any further rent to the plaintiff who, accordingly, was forced to file a Money Suit in 1953 for realisation of rent from the defendants in the Court of a Munsif at Narayanganj. In the said suit the defendants asserted that they were not tenants under the plaintiff and on the contrary alleged to have purchased the suit property by a registered deed of sale executed by Modhusudan Saha on, the 15th September, 1953 on the basis of an agreement for sale executed by him on the 1st July, 1951. The plaintiff therefore, withdrew the said Money Suit on 20-4-54 and on 11-3-59 filed the present suit for declaration of his title and recovery of possession and mesne profits. The defendant’s No. 1 and 2 contested the suit on the same grounds as were set up by them in the Money Suit. They denied that they had occupied the premises under Modhusudan as his tenants or under the plaintiff. The learned Judges of the High Court, in dismissing the suit on appeal, made the following observations at the outset:

"The main plank of the plaintiff's case is Ext. 4, a Bharanama, alleged to have been executed by one of the defendants, Sashi Mohan Saha, in favour of Modhusudan on 27-8-49 when Sashi Mohan and his brother Lal Mohan came to occupy two rooms of the suit properties as tenants at rental of Rs. 125/-. If the plaintiff can establish Ext. 4, then the defendant's case of coming into occupation of the properties in question on the basis of Ext. 'A', the deed of agreement dated 1-7-51, falls to the ground."

3. Thereafter the learned Judges held that as the document Ext. 4 was not put   to Shashi Mohan Saha when he came to the witness box to depose and he was not given an opportunity to explain the admission contained therein, as is required under the provision of section 145 of the Evidence Act, the said document had not been legally proved and, in support of the said view, relied upon the judgment of a Full Bench of the Lahore High Court in case of Firm Malik Das Raj Faquir Chand Vs. Firm Piara Lal Ayaram reported in A.I.R. 1946 (Lah.) 65. The question involved in this appeal, therefore, is the scope and extent of the applicability of section 145 of the Evidence Act and whether this section is attracted in case of an admission.

4. Mr. S.R. Pal appearing for the appellant contended that there is a distinction between the use of previous statement of a witness for the purpose of contradicting him in which case his attention is required to be drawn to that under section 145 of the Evidence Act and the use of previous statement as a piece of substantive evidence under some sections of the Evidence Act in which case the question of applicability of section 145 of the Evidence Act does not arise.

<u>5. Section 145 lays down that a witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing, but that if it is intended to contradict him by the writing, his attention must be drawn to that part of the previous statement by which it is intended to contradict him. This is to be done to afford an opportunity to the witness to explain the inconsistency between the statement made in the Court and his previous statement. The previous statement made by the witness is not substantive evidence and it cannot be used to prove the existence of a relevant fact. These are, however, exceptions to this rule. The statement of a person who is dead or who cannot be found, or who has become incapable of giving the evidence or whose attendance cannot be procured, when admitted in evidence under section 32 of the Evidence Act, becomes substantive evidence. Similarly evidence given in a judicial proceeding or before a person authorised by law to take it, when admitted in evidence under section 33 of the Evidence Act, becomes substantive evidence. So also the evidence of a witness in a criminal case given by him in the committing Court, when brought under section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on record of the Sessions Court, may be used as substantive evidence at the trial. Though a previous statement made by a witness cannot be used as substantive evidence it can, nevertheless, be used under section 145 of the Evidence Act to contradict him for the purpose of which his attention must be drawn to that part of his previous statement which is in conflict with his evidence.</u>

<u>Admission, on the other hand, are themselves, substantive evidence. Section 17 of the Evidence Act defines an admission and sections 18-20 mention the persons by whom admissions may be made and the circumstances under which they may be made. Section 21 renders an admission relevant and probable against the person who makes them in the cases mentioned therein. It will appear from what have been stated above that the use to which a previous statement can be put by taking recourse to section 145 of the Evidence Act is different from the purpose for which it is sought to be used as an admission under section 17 and 21 of the Evidence Act. In the former case the utility of the previous statement lies in contradicting the maker thereof and shaking his credibility while in the latter case it is utilised as substantive evidence. It is only when the veracity of a witness is sought to be impeach that the need for drawing his attention to his previous statement arises, but when the previous statement is sought to be utilised as substantive evidence, the question of drawing the attention of the witness to that statement does not arise.</u>

<u>The view expressed above finds support from the view expressed by M. Monir (former Chief Justice, Supreme Court of Pakistan) at page 60 of his book "Principles and Digest of the Law of Evidence'' printed in 1969. According to the learned author, "Section 145 does not apply to admissions. An admission is admissible proprio vigore and is given in evidence as substantive evidence and not for contradiction purpose". The Supreme Court of India, in the case of Bharat Singh and others Vs. Mst. Bhagirathi reported in A.I.R. 1966 (S.C.) 405 expressed itself fully on the point in the following passage :—</u>

<u>"Admissions are substantive evidence by themselves, in view of sections 17 and 21 of the Indian Evidence Act, though they are not conclusive proof of the matters admitted. We are of opinion that the admissions duly proved are admissible evidence irrespective of whether the party making them appeared in the witness box or not and whether that party when appearing as witness was confronted with those statements in case it made a statement contrary to those admissions. The purpose of contradicting the witness under section 145 of the Evidence Act is very different from the purpose of proving the admission. Admission is substantive evidence of the fact admitted while a previous statement used to contradict a witness does not become substantive evidence and merely serves the purpose of throwing doubt on the veracity of the witness."</u>

<u>The decision of the Full Bench of the Lahore High Court in the case of Firm Malik Das Raj Vs. Firm Peary Lal, reported in A.I.R. 1946 (Lahore) 65, was taken note of both by M. Monir in his book and the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of India in the case referred to above and they opined that the observation of the Privy Council in the case of Balgangadhar Tilok Vs. Srinivash Pandit reported in 42 Indian Appeal, 135 upon which the decision of the Lahore High Court was based, is no authority for the view that when an admission is sought to be proved., it must be put to the party making it to enable it to explain the admission, as the question of use of admission did not directly arise in the case of Balgangadhar Tilok.</u>

<u>In the instant case the plaintiff-appellant wanted to use the document Ext. 4 executed by D.W. 7 Sashi Mohan Sana, defendant No. 1, as substantive evidence by way of admission in support of his case that the premises in dispute was taken on rent from Modhusudan Sana, father of P.W. 1 Krishnadhan Saha. The question of using that document to contradict D.W. 7 did not arise and hence the necessity of drawing the attention of the said witness to the statement in the said document, under section 145 of the Evidence Act, did not arise. The learned Judges of the High Court, accordingly, fell into an error in holding that the said document could not be taken into consideration.</u>

It appears that the finding of the learned Judges of the High Court in the appeal was, to a large extent, influenced by the qution whether document Ext. 4 was entitled to be considered. Since we have arrived at the conclusions that they were not justified in discarding the said document from consideration, we think that for proper disposal of the appeal that was filed in the High Court, the said document should be considered along with other evidence on record, both oral and documentary. The case should, therefore, go back to the High Court Division for disposal of the appeal in accordance with the law.

The appeal is accordingly allowed and the judgment of the High Court is set aside. The case is sent back on remand for disposal of the appeal in the light of what have been stated above. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

parties:
United Liner Agencies of Pakistan Limited, Ctg.  ------- Appellant. 
Vs. 
Ehram Jute Baling, Narayanganj, and ors  ------- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 17-8-66 passed by the Dacca High Court in F.A.No.103 of 1961)
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, J.—Appellants, who are plaintiffs, have obtained Special Leave from the decision of the Dacca High Court passed on appeal. Plaint case is that appellants in the capacity of Clearing and Forwarding Agent of defendant-respondents for shipment of certain bales of Jute abroad (Germany) incurred sundry expenses on account of the respondents  and became entitled to remuneration. Bills were submitted to respondents in the ordinary course of business and a sum of Rs.12,212/76p. demanded. Respondents first issued two cheques but later counter manded. In their written statement respondents admitted the claim of appellants, but set up a claim of set off to the extent of Rs.13,434/- on account of damages for loss of 50 bales of jute carried in Flat belonging to R. S. N. & Co. Ltd., and I. G. N. B. and Co. Ltd. from Narayanganj to Chalna and again from Chafna to Narayanganj.

2. Record shows aforesaid 50 bales out of the total cargo shipped by the respondents, could not be cleared and forwarded by the appellants at Chalna for their carriage abroad by Sea going vessel. They were rejected by overseas Vessel, as some were found wet and water-stained. Respondents rebooked the said discarded bales for carriage by the aforesaid carriers for stetting, them back. The Inland Carrier Steamer Company carried the jute in question from Chalna to Narayanganj and inforired respondents of the arrival of the same at Narayanganj. Dispute arose between appellants and respondents for the collection of the said bales, respondents demanding flat receipts, but appellants insisting on prior payment of their outstanding dues before parting with them. The result was that jute bales were not cleared. Parties resorted to court claiming and counter claiming by way of set-off.

3. The parties went to trail on two issues : (1) Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to claim the plaint amount, and (2) Whether the defendants were entitled to set-off the amount claimed by them. On consideration of evidence, oral and documentary, the trial Judge held that plaintiffs succeeded in proving their claim on which there was no challenge, and refused the claim of set-off on the ground that the amount was not ascertained and the carrier was not made a party to the suit. He, however, found negligence on the part of plaintiffs. He decreed the suit with costs.

4. On appeal by defendants, a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court found, that though plaintiffs' claim was not disputed by defendants, they were entitled to set-off. The trial Judge's finding that the amount was not an ascertained sum was reversed, holding that defendants in their writ ten statement mentioned a specific amount and paid court fee thereon, and since the plaintiffs having opportunity to challenge the claim, filed no objection and led no evidence, the amount claimed by defendants was an ascertained sum within the meaning of Older VIII, Rule 6 of the Code. As to the lack of carrier being made a party, it was held that from the evidence, it was clear that defendants proved, that plaintiffs were solely responsible for the loss. The carrier v as therefore not a necessary party. The High Court allowed the set-off against the plaintiffs for Rs.1, 221-3-9.

5. Against this judgment and the decree, plaintiff-appellants have obtained special ease. Two questions are involved in this appeal : (1) In view of the fact that to claim set off under Order VIII, Rule 6, the amount shall have to be an ascertained sum, could the claim of defendants unliquidated damages for the loss of bales be said to be an ascertained sum ? And (2) whether fur the determination of liability of appellants in respect of damages, the carrier is a necessary patty.

6. Mr. Hafizullah, has appeared on behalf of the appellants and Mr. Moinul Huq for the respondents. Both have advanced their respective arguments and they will be taken up in their appropriate places, as and when they arise in dealing with the questions set out above.

7. Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Counsel for the appellants challenges the finding of the High Court, citing authorities in his favour, that the amount of damages claimed in the written statement as set off, was an ascertained sum of money. He argues referring to Order VIII, rule 6, of the Code of Civil Procedure, that any specified amount in the written statement claimed by way of damages, even though arising from the same transaction, is not an ascertained sum of money. He says, what is claimed by respondents is nothing but unliquidated damages for breach of contract. Even if, plaintiffs have not challenged that amount, still then the court has to adjudicate the amount of damages, in fact, defendants are entitled to which can be set-off. He says, mere omission to file an objection by plaintiffs will not convert an unliquidated damages into an ascertained sum. Mr. Moinul Huq, for the respondents, has found it difficult to repeal the contention of Mr. Hafizullah. He, however, argues that in the circumstances of the case, when plaintiffs did not challenge the claim of set-off by filing additional plaint in reply, nor did they call for any evidence in rebuttal to the testimony of the proprietor defendant, so in the context of the facts, the amount claimed in the written statement can now be treated as ascertained sum and the High Court was justified in so holding.

<u>8. On a comparison of rival contentions, we find that the submission of Mr. Hafizullah has great force. Defendants no doubt claimed specified sum and paid full court-fee thereon. Plaintiffs under the Code, had an opportunity of filing additional plaint in reply, disputing the claim of set-off but did not take any steps. At the trial defendants led oral evidence in support of their claim made in the written statement. The averment was made by the second defendant, the proprietor of the first defendant. He was not cross-examined, nor any witness called by plaintiffs in rebuttal to this statement. Could it then be said that in this context, the amount claimed by defendants, has become an ascertained sum of money as contemplated in rule 6, Order VIII of the Code ? The rule says, that when set-off is claimed, the written statement shall he treated as a plaint. For defendants to get a decree on this claim of set off, the Court has to adjudicate, and defendants are to satisfy it that they, in fact, suffered loss claimed by them, and they are to establish it on evidence. It not divided that the contract of carriage between plaintiffs and defendants did not contain any clause stipulating any sum as liquidated damages. The amount claimed by defendants is unliquidated damages. There is a string of authorities holding, that unliquidated damages are not an ascertained sum of money within the meaning of rule 6 of Order VIII. To cite only a few of them : Edward Dalgleish Vs. Ramdin Singh Choudhury 14 C.W.N. 170, Diltor Koer Vs. Harkhoo Singh A.I.R. 1916 Patna 167, Har Parsad Vs. Firm Ram Sarup Radha A.I.R. 1924 Allahabad 872, Pir Baksh Vs. Rameshwar Nath A.I.R. 1929 Allahabad 52, Galstaun Vs. Radhakissen A.I.R. 1931 Calcutta 23, Bhikanarao Vs. Sridhar A.I.R. 1931 Nagpur 12.</u>

9. There is also authority for the proposition, that "ascertained sum" does not mean a sum admitted by the plaintiff. Cases of Edward Dalgleish and Bhikanarao may be cited on this point. Consequently, the view of the High Court cannot be sustained. The contention of Mr. Hafizullah that the amount claimed by defendants  is unliquidated damages, and is not an ascertained sum of money within the meaning of Rule 6, Order VIII of the Code is well founded and must prevail.

10. Mr. Moinul Huq, however, has alternatively set up the claim of equitable set off. Mr. Hafizullah has felt it difficult to meet the point. A reference to Order 20, rule 19(3) clearly indicates that the Code, though has not expressly provided for equitable set off, yet has kept a margin for its application by using words `or otherwise' in this rule. The application of rule of equitable set-off is to be gathered from leading judicial authorities. We propose to refer to only those authorities where the rule has been applied to facts analogous to the present case. In the present case, we find that plaintiffs undertook to carry certain bales of jute for shipment abroad for defendants, the shippers. In the course of fulfillment of this contract the claim and counter claim of set-off have arisen.

<u>11. It is now well settled that equitable set-off can be claimed when both cross demands, claim and sot off, arise out of the same transaction. It is true that equitable set-off cannot be claimed as of right, and the court has a discretion either to allow or not to allow it. If protracted enquiry is necessary, it may be a good ground for refusal. Equitable set-off cannot be claimed, when it does not arise from the same or cognate transaction.</u>

12. Turning from principle to authorities; we find Brojendra Nath Das Vs. The Budge-Budge Jute Mill Company, Limited I. L. R. 20 Calcutta 528, is a decision of Special Bench of the Calcutta High Court on a reference of the year 1893. In a suit in the Calcutta Small Cause Court to recover Rs.1,197-5-6- the price of goods sold and delivered, the defendants claimed to set off a sum of Rs.2,738-4-0 being the loss which they had sustained by reason of the plaintiff's breach of contract, it was held that the defendants claim was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Small Cause Court, but their claim by way of equitable set off was sustainable. The relevant passage may be quoted:

"A series of cases in all the courts of India has established that what is called an equitable right of set-off exists in this country when both the claim of the plaintiff and that of the defendant arise out of same transaction, though the claim sought to be set off is not within the provisions of section Ill of the Code of Civil Procedure

13. In Girdharilar Chaturbhuj Vs. Surajmal A.I.R. 1940 Nagpur 177, it has been held that equitable set-off cannot be claimed as a matter of right, and the court has discretion to say that it should not be allowed, where a protracted enquiry is needed for the determination of the sum due. In Sarangdhar Singh Vs. Lakshmi Narayan A.I.R. 1955 Patna 320. It has been held there can be equitable set-off in respect of an ascertained sum of money, but the essence of such claim is that there must be some connection between the plaintiff's claim for debt, and the defendant's claim to set-off, which will make it inequitable to drive the defendant to a separate suit, as, for instance when they arise out of the same transaction or transactions which can be regarded as one transaction or where there is a knowledge on both sides of an existing debt due to one party and a credit by the other party founded on and trusting to such a debt as a means of discharging it.

14. In Hari Ananda Vs. Muhammad Esahak 40 C.W.N. 751, R. C. Mitter J. has held that equitable set-off can be claimed not only in respect of unascertained amount, but also in respect of ascertained amount. But in order that a claim for equitably set-off may arise, it is not sufficient that there are cross demands, it is further necessary that there should be a connection between them which makes it inequitable to drive the defendant to a separate suit, when the demands arise out of the same transaction or when there is on each side knowledge of and confidence in one debt discharging the other.

15. In Morgan Vs. Martin Johnson 1948(2) All England Law Reports 196, the facts were that the plaintiffs issued a writ under R.S.C., Order 14, claiming against the defendants charges for storage of vehicles and for telephone calls. The defendants admitted the claim, but contended that the plaintiffs had broken the terms of the contract of storage, by delivering up a vehicle to some one otherwise than in accordance with the contract, or, alternatively, that the plaintiffs had acted in breach of their duty as bailees by keeping so inefficient a watch on the vehicle, that it was stolen. The defendants, accordingly, claimed a set off to the extent of the whole of the plaintiffs claim, and a counter claim to the extent to which the damages for breach of contract or for negligence exceeded the amount of the plaintiffs claim. The Master ordered that the plaintiffs should be at liberty to sign final judgment on the claim, with a stay of execution pending the trial of the set-off and counter-claim, and this order was confirmed by the Judge in Chambers with a variation allowing stay of execution until trial of the counter-claim or further order. From this order the defendants appealed and it was held that since the defendants set-off and counter-claim disclosed an equitable set off, which by virtue of the Judicature Act, 1925, would constitute a good defence to the action, the proper order was that the defendants should have unconditional leave to defend and not that there should be judgment for the plaintiffs with a stay of execution.

16. In Bhupendra Narayan Vs. Bahadur Singh A.I.R. 1952 Supreme Court 201, it has been held that plea in the nature of equitable set-off is not available when the cross-demands do not arise out of the same transaction.

<u>17. In Eastern Federal Union Insurance Co. Ltd., Vs. Quarashi Brothers 18 D.L.R. 62, a Single Judge of the Dacca High Court has held that equitable set-off cannot be claimed as a matter of right. When an investigation is required for ascertaining the amount of loss, it should not be allowed. It may be stated that the learned Judge though, has referred to a decision of the Bombay High Court in Doison and Barlow Ltd. Vs. Bengal Spitting and Wearing Company I.L.R. 21 Bombay 126, yet it seems, that he has over stated the rule regarding investigation in claim for equitable set-off. The Bombay case refused equitable set-off also, as the investigation would have considerably delayed the matter. The authorities indicate that where a protected enquiry is necessary, the court may not exercise its discretion in allowing equitable set-off. But the learned Single Judge has used the expression ‘investigation’ unqualified. This unqualified use of the word ‘investigation’ cannot be approved.</u>

<u>A review of authorities shows that the view expressed therein are in accord with the view we have taken on the question of equitable set off.</u>

<u>18. Turning to facts, we find that defendants claim to set-off arose out of a contract of carriage of Jute and in course of fulfillment of that contract, claim and counter claim by way of set-off have arisen. Defendant's claim, therefore, has arisen from the same transaction and though the amount claimed by the defendants by way of set-off for the loss of 50 bales due to negligence plaintiffs cannot in terms of rule 6 of Order VIII be said to be an ascertained sum of money, the amount of damage being unliquidated damages, defendants can claim equitable set-off of the said sum. The conclusion of the High Court that the defendants claim of set-off can In sustained stands but not on the reasons given by it, but on those set out above.</u>

<u>19. The second question is whether set off is maintainable without the carrier being made a party, or in other words, whether carrier is a necessary party. At this stage it is appropriate to look at the rule of Shipping or Forwarding Agent's liability. The liability of a Shipping or Clearing and Forwarding Agent depends upon the terms of the contract between the shipper and the agent. But there are certain implied terms which govern the relation between the parties when one acts as such Shipping or Forwarding Agent. They have been succinctly described in Senators on Charter Parties and Bill of Lading. The High Court has referred to the relevant passage at page 47 of the 16th Edition of the Book. It may be reproduced :</u>

<u>"Although the same firm or company will act both as loading broker and forwarding agent, the two function are quite distinct. The forwarding agent, unlike the loading broker, acts on behalf of the shipper and his normal duties are to ascertain the date and place of sailing, obtain a space allocation if that is required, prepare the bill of lading and send the draft to the Lading broker, arrange for the goods to be brought alongside, make the custom entry and pay any dues and collect the signed bill of lading after shipment. Although not himself a carrier a forwarding agent may also sometime assume liability of carrying. On the other hand, a ship owner, may by the term of his bill of lading limit his liability to that of a forwarding agent for land carriage beyond the port of discharge."</u>

20. Liabilities that a shipping or forwarding agent may incur can be gathered from a decision of Rawlatt, J. in the case of Jones Vs. European and General Express Company in Aspinall's Reports of Maritime cases vol. 15, 138. The facts were that in July 1918 the plaintiff forwarded to the defendants, who were shipping agents, eight bales of cloth to be shipped to a French port and thence to be forwarded by rail to a consignee at Lyons. The defendants undertook to have the goods insured against pilferage during transit from warehouse to warehouse. They held an open policy of insurance under which they were able to declare the goods in question and obtain the protection of the underwriter's undertaking. The defendants made the usual and proper arrangements with steamships and railways for the carriage of the goods in question to their destination, and also made proper arrangements with the underwriters for the insurance of the goods during transit. While the goods were in the custody of the French Customs authorities, two bales were lost, and only six bales reached their destination. It was thought that the two bales were stolen. There was no evidence of any negligence or default on the part of the defendants having caused the loss of the goods. It was held, that the obligation imposed upon the defendants was, not to carry the goods, but to make arrangements with the carriers, and to make such arrangement as might be necessary for the intermediate steps in the journey between the different sets of carriers and others who had successive possession of the goods.

21. As to the contract to insure, the defendants were only obliged to place the plaintiffs' risk with the underwriters, for whose subsequent actions they were not responsible.

22. In discharging these obligations the defendants had shown no negligence. It was further observed that the plaintiff could independently recover from the defendants, if he could make out that the loss was due to defendants negligence in carrying out what they were instructed to do.

<u>23. From the authorities referred to above, it is manifest, that shipping agent or forwarding agent or Clearing and Forwarding Agent does incur liability to the shipper for negligence in carrying out what he is asked to do. It is true a contract of carriage does involve the carrier but then the liability of the Forwarding Agent and the carrier as against the shipper will depend upon the facts of each case. It cannot be denied that the carrier is a proper party, but whether he is a necessary party will depend, whether plaintiff is claiming damages independently from the Forwarding Agent for his negligence in discharging his duties as such agent. In such circumstances carrier is just a proper party but not a necessary party, so that the suit will not fail in his absence.</u>

24. It is to be remembered that plaintiffs did not raise the question of defect of parties in their pleading, even though they got opportunity to do so. They called no evidence to show that the carrier was in any way concerned with the claim of damages set up by defendants. The evidence in this regard is of defendants alone. The question was agitated at the time of argument only. In this background the learned Judges of the High Court have found that 83 bales of jute were shipped on 24-7-57 and it was on 13-11-57 that the plaintiffs' asked the defendants to collect flat receipts of 42 missing bales, and so the defendants asserted that the value of the goods deteriorated because of the gross negligence of plaintiffs. The learned Judges referred to the evidence of second defendant, the proprietor of the first defendant, and held that he had expressly asserted that he claimed the amount of Rs.13,434/- from plaintiffs, for the total loss of jute and that plaintiffs were responsible for it. Loss accrued due to their negligence and that handling was also a part of the duty of the agent. It was found there was no cross-examination of the witness. It was held that plaintiffs as Forwarding agent were responsible for the dispatch of goods from Chalna to Chittagong, and also for the custody of jute while lying at port either in barge or jetty sheds. Both the High Court and the trial Court concurrently held plaintiffs guilty of gross negligence in refusing to hand over flat receipts which would have enabled defendants, to recover the missing 50 hales of jute, and so defendants suffered loss which the plaintiffs were liable to make good. On facts, therefore, the appellants have an insurmountable hurdle to overcome. This finding cannot be challenged at this stage in this division. This finding of fact concludes the second question. The High Court was perfectly justified in holding that on facts, the carrier was not a necessary party. We have held that carrier is a proper party. The claim of defendants therefore cannot fail in the absence of the Carter in the particular facts of the present case The point raised by the appellants fails.

In the result, this appeal is dismissed, but having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, we make no order as to costs.

End.
